chunk_context.text:
The sign formed a T; the intersection formed a T; and a T-shaped mark was hastily drawn on the door of the victim's house, not far from the intersection. It was a crazy idea to form a T with a person.
The local police were at a loss. Van was eccentric but a quiet, harmless man. He had no enemies and no friends. His only friend was a simple man named Clinton, who had been playing the role of Van's servant. Clinton had disappeared, and according to the evidence that was not made public, the district attorney, Crummett of Hampshire County, believed that this servant was another victim of the bloodthirsty maniac who had written a chapter in the modern American crime chronicle.
There were more similar reports, including details of the unfortunate principal's rural life in Arroyo, bits of information gathered by the police about Van and Clinton's last known whereabouts, and the district attorney's exaggerated announcement.
Ellery took off his glasses, wiped them, and put them back on, scanning the terrible relics left at the scene with sharp eyes.
Near the top of the signpost's arms, there were many small holes left by the police who had dug out the nails. Each hole was surrounded by an irregular rust-brown stain, and thin brown streaks slowly seeped out of the hole, which were the blood that had flowed from the victim's injured hands. There were two more holes on the signpost's arms that extended out, with edges that were not clearly visible, left by the nails that had been driven in to support the body in the armpits. The entire signpost was covered in dried blood, forming a crisscross pattern, very dirty. This blood flowed down from the victim's neck, which was cracked near the top of the signpost.

Thus, it was not until July 1st, eight days after Inspector Vane received a telegram from Megalas, that the Helen approached the Long Island coast. Port authorities made arrangements for it to quickly pass through New York Harbor. The Helen, after a brief delay, was accompanied by a police boat and several small vessels as it entered Long Island Sound. These small vessels were hired by ambitious reporters who found it difficult to leave the Helen's deck, which had been polished with a grindstone [1].
Eight days... Eight days of calm and uneventful sailing. Even the funeral was a calm affair. Brad was buried in a rather unimpressive cemetery on Long Island, or rather, in an unsuitable environment. The press noticed that Mrs. Brad displayed remarkable fortitude in bearing this severe test. Even her daughter, who had no blood ties to the deceased, displayed more grief at the funeral than the widow herself.
The search for Werger Croscak was expanded into a nationwide manhunt. His physical description was sent to all police departments and county sheriffs' offices across the United States, as well as to all port officials; he was under surveillance by police in all forty-eight states, Canada, and Mexico. Despite the large net, no blackfish was caught; the man disappeared without a trace, as if he had flown into the sky from the ground. There was no trace of Clinton either.

chunk_context.text:
"No, but my grandfather and his family converted. Apparently, they did so after returning from China, and they were very devout."
"They must have faced discrimination too?"
"Yes, quite a lot. Being Orthodox, they seemed to be under even more pressure."
"Orthodox. That's rare."
"When talking about Christians in Japan, they are usually Catholics or Protestants. They are often referred to as old religions and new religions."
"Greek Orthodoxy appeared long before the religious reform. In the 11th century, Christianity split into Greek Orthodoxy and the Roman Catholic Church due to arguments over idolatry. After the fall of the Byzantine Empire, Russian Orthodoxy continued to spread from Russia. However, Japan has been more influenced by Western culture in history, so although there are relics such as Tokyo's St. Nicholas Church, the number is small."
"It was probably influenced by the Manchurian Russians."
"This is also related to Medvedev's requiem."
"So, what about the funeral?"
"He was placed in a stone coffin and placed in the mortuary."
"Is it in this house?"
"Not quite, it's not something pleasant. It's about 100 meters away." Kaname sighed.
"Akuhaba is there too..."
"No," Kaname denied, "my father always saw Orthodoxy as a Western thing and disliked it. He didn't even like us going near the church."
Comparing Akuobashi's character, it's understandable.
"However, the church couldn't be demolished while my grandfather was alive."
"So, it's going to be demolished soon?"
"Yes, it's on the church's side."
"I see."
After leaving the window, Muketsumi picked up the dusty Medvedev record and said, "Excuse me, can you take me to the church?"
From the trend of the conversation, it was inevitable for him to say that.
From the entrance hall, turning right leads to a short, dark passage where you can't see the end. It is said that the church is at the end of this passage.

"It's possible. In 1919, when Medvedev stayed in the city of Sparrow, the assassination of the Tsar family was widely reported both domestically and internationally. At that time, the vast fortune of the world's richest family, the Romanovs, disappeared, and only Medvedev knew about it. It would have been easy to kill him and take the fortune for themselves.
"And this time period coincides with the rapid growth of the company, which is quite interesting."
"But what does this have to do with Kumagai-san?"
The inspector seemed to sense that McCarto was changing the subject and urged him to continue.
"So, did the one who wrote his own requiem, Medvedev, have any descendants?"
"According to my investigation, he had a woman in Japan who was like a mistress. When Medvedev's body was found, she was already pregnant. She has not been heard from since then, and the child she carried should now be around seventy years old. In other words, does Medvedev have any grandsons or great-grandchildren?"
"You're saying that Kumagai-san is?"
"It's possible. If he believed his great-grandfather was killed by the Inagaki family, if he turned into a devil and swore revenge at the grave of his great-grandfather, to wipe out the Inagaki family."
"Is he really Medvedev's great-grandson?" Detective Jouji clenched his fists and leaned forward to ask.
McArthur shrugged: "This is where you come in to investigate. I was just giving an example. Of course, this is the most reliable scenario."
McArthur leaned back in his chair, as if announcing that everything was over. The sense of exhaustion even infected me.
"That's all I have to say."
With these words, McArthur's thirty-minute speech came to an end, accompanied by a tragic, legendary conclusion.
No one spoke a word.
The unexpected conclusion left everyone speechless. It was not a conclusion that could be believed just because it was said.
However, no one could offer an effective rebuttal.

relation.subject: Hercule Poirot

evidence.quote: I haven't thought about solving any cases.
Eleanor Marshall was clearly meeting someone

relation.why_cross_chunk: His holiday denial contrasts with later investigative observation of a suspected rendezvous.

verifier.reason: Poirot denies professional purpose; later observation shows investigative attention to Eleanor's rendezvous.

chunk_context.text:
"I've been looking forward to meeting Miss Dunn. I buy a lot of things at Rossmond's, and I'm sure she's the owner, isn't she? I think she's a charming woman, how well she dresses, how well she puts together an outfit that makes her look so good. The outfit I wore last night was bought from her store. I think, from any angle, she's a lovely woman."
Colonel Barron, sitting next to Miss Bustard, had been shamelessly staring at the swimsuit models, and he muttered, "She seems like a refined woman."
Mrs. Gardner continued to knit her needles, "Honestly, Mr. Poirot, seeing you here has given me an idea - not that I'm not excited to see you, because I am, and Mr. Gardner knows it - but I can't help but wonder, you know, that you might be here for professional reasons. You understand what I mean, don't you? Oh, I'm just too sensitive, Mr. Gardner will tell you how sensitive I am, and if I get involved in any crime, I can't stand it. You know -"
"You know, Mr. Poirot, Mrs. Gardner is very sensitive."
Hercule Poirot waved his hand in the air. "Then rest assured, madam, my purpose here is the same as yours - to relax and enjoy a holiday. I haven't thought about solving any cases."
"There are no bodies on Pirate Island," said Miss Bustle stiffly.
"Ah, that may not be the case," said Hercule Poirot, pointing to the beach below. "Look at them, lying there in rows. What do they look like? Men and women? They look like nothing but - bodies[2]!"
"They look pretty good, some of them are quite attractive, though some are a bit thin," said Major Barry appreciatively.

Poirot did not believe that the woman known as Eleanor Steward would ever want to be alone in her life. A man like Hercule Poirot, who had seen so much, knew it at once. How could it be otherwise? Eleanor Marshall was clearly meeting someone, and Poirot knew very well who that person would be – at least he thought he did.
However, he soon realized that he was wrong on this point. Just after the raft had rounded the headland and disappeared, Patrick Redfern and Kenneth Marshall emerged from the hotel and walked down the beach together.
Marshall nodded to Poirot. "Good morning, Poirot. Have you seen my wife?"
Poirot replied evasively, "Is she up so early?"
Marshall said, "She's not in her room." He looked up at the sky. "It's a beautiful day, I should go swimming now. I have a lot to do this morning."
Patrick Redfern, meanwhile, scanned the beach. He sat down next to Poirot, waiting for his intended. Poirot asked, "Where is your wife, Redfern? Is she up early too?"
Patrick Redfern said, "Christine? Oh, she's gone out painting. She's been quite taken with art lately." He spoke with an air of impatience, clearly distracted. As time passed, he grew increasingly agitated, clearly waiting for Eleanor to appear. He turned at the sound of footsteps, hoping it was Eleanor emerging from the hotel.
He was disappointed time and again. First came the Gardners with their knitting and books, followed by Miss Bustle. Mrs. Gardner continued her industrious work, sitting down in her chair and immediately starting to knit while she chatted nonstop.
"Poirot sir, it seems unusually quiet on the beach this morning. Where has everyone gone?"
Poirot replied that the families with children had gone out to sea in their boats, likely to spend the day there.
"Ah, that explains the quiet. Only one person is swimming this morning, Mr. Marshall."

chunk_context.text:
Although she had enjoyed her time abroad, it was nice to leave the Women's Royal Naval Service and become a free woman again. The job had been interesting, with various social events and amusing, yet there were also tedious routines and the feeling of being confined with her comrades, which sometimes made her want to escape.
It was during that time that she longed for Wormsley Valley and this shabby yet cool and comfortable house, and her dear mother.
Lyn had a love-hate relationship with her mother. When she was far away from home, she loved her more, and the annoying things were put aside, and even if she remembered them, they only made her more homesick. Dear mother, she could drive you crazy! If only she didn't have to listen to her mother's voice, so sweet and melodious, but full of complaints, pronouncing the same old clichés over and over again.
She was here now, having completed her service, free, and back in White House. She had been home for three days, and an inexplicable dissatisfaction and restlessness were creeping up on her. Everything was the same - almost unchanged - the house, her mother, Rolly, the farm, and the family. The only thing that was different and shouldn't be was herself...
"Darling..." Mrs. Marchmont's delicate call came from downstairs. "Would you like me to bring a tray of breakfast to your room?"
Lynn called out loudly:
"No, thank you. I'll come down."
"Why," she thought, "mom insists on saying 'my daughter.' That's too silly!"

Indeed, they all relied on Gordon Claude. This did not mean that any family member was a parasite or idle. Jeremy Claude was a senior partner in a law firm, and Lionel Claude was a practicing physician.
However, behind the routine work and ordinary days, there was a solid financial cushion that made people feel comfortable. There was never a need for thrift or saving. The future was secure. Gordon Claude, a widower without children, would take care of everything. He had told everyone, and not just once, that it was a done deal.
His widowed sister, Adela Marchmont, might have moved into a smaller, more manageable house, but she stayed in the White House. Lin En attended elite schools. She had the opportunity to accept any expensive training she desired, thanks to the regular checks from her Gordon uncle.
Everything was so stable and safe, until Gordon Claude's unexpected marriage.
"Of course, dear," Adele continued, "we were all surprised. If there was one thing that seemed certain, it was that Gordon would never marry again, you know. He seemed to have many family ties and familial relationships."
Yes, Lynn thought, there were already enough relatives. Perhaps sometimes it would feel a little too much?
"He was always so kind and friendly," Mrs. Marchmont continued, "although he could be a little domineering at times. He never liked to eat at a table that was polished to a shine, always insisting that I put down an old-fashioned tablecloth. In fact, he even sent me a most beautiful Venetian lace tablecloth from Italy."
"It's certainly to his advantage to indulge his whims," Lynn said dryly. She then asked curiously, "How did he meet his...second wife? You didn't tell me in your letter."

"Undoubtedly. You really know everything! Honestly, I was terrified. I had to think of something. After I'd phoned Lynn, I walked five miles to Dersley and caught the milk train back to London. I just managed to make my bed look rumpled and have breakfast with Rosemary. I never thought the police would suspect her."
"Of course, I had no idea who killed him! I couldn't imagine anyone who would want to kill him. As far as I know, besides myself and Rosalind, there was no one with a motive to kill."
"This," said Poirot, "has always been a tricky puzzle. Motive. You and your sister had a motive to kill Jardine, and every member of the de Clercy family had a motive to kill your sister."
David exclaimed:
"So, she was killed? Not by suicide?"
"No. It was a well-thought-out, premeditated crime. One of the packets of bromide sleeping powder was switched for morphine – the one at the bottom of the box."
"In the sleeping pills," David frowned. "You don't mean—you don't mean Leonel Claude, do you?"
"No," said Poirot. "You see, any member of the Claude family could have switched the sleeping pills for morphine. Aunt Cassie could have done it before they left the consulting room. Rolly had brought butter and eggs to Rosalind at Frohman's. Mrs. Marchmont had been there. Mrs. Jeremy Claude had been there. Even Lynn Marchmont had been there. And they all had motives."
"Lynn had no motive," David called out.
"We all had motives," said Lynn.

None of the typists are working.'"
The blonde girl continued:
"And then I said, 'It's not our fault, Miss Martin.'"
"What did Miss Martin say?"
"Well, she didn't believe us at first," the brunette girl said. "She said, 'Nonsense, you're just repeating the silly gossip from the store. It must be someone else. Why would it be Ina?' Then she strode back to her office and called the police station, and found out it was true."
"But I don't understand," said Janet almost in a daze. "I don't understand who would want to kill Ina?"
"It's not because of a boyfriend, she seems not to have one," said the brunette girl.

"Big or small, they're all the same to me!" He closed his eyes and shuddered. "It's awful to be rocking on the sea."
"Thank goodness, the sea is calm today, like a pond."
Poirot replied decisively, "There's no such thing as a truly calm ocean. There will always be waves, there will always be waves."
"If you ask my opinion," said Colonel Barry, "most people who get seasick do so because of their own minds."
"That's what a sailor would say," the clergyman said with a smile, "isn't it, Colonel?"
"I've only been seasick once," said Colonel Barry, "when crossing the English Channel. I just ignore it."
"It's strange how seasickness can affect some people and not others," said Miss Bustle thoughtfully, "it's so unfair, and it has nothing to do with a person's general health. Some sick people don't get seasick at all. I've heard that it has something to do with one's spine. The same thing can be said for acrophobia. I'm not very good at heights, but Mrs. Redfern is even worse. The other day, on the cliff-top path to Harford, she was so dizzy she could barely walk and held onto me tightly. She told me that once, when she was walking down the steps outside the Milan Cathedral, she got halfway and couldn't go any further, leaving her stuck in the middle. She hadn't thought about it when she was climbing up, but coming down was a different story."
"She'd better not go near the steps at Elves' Bay then," said Lane. "They're very steep."
Miss Burrage made a face. "I wouldn't go up them myself. They're more for young people. The Conyngham boys and the Masterton children, they love running up and down them, having the time of their lives."
"Mrs. Redfern has come over," said Lane. "She's just been swimming."

"I turned to the page that was open, which talked about various ways of killing, such as making a wax effigy to represent the victim and then slowly melting it with heat - or using a needle to pierce the wax effigy's heart, which would cause the person to die. Later, I heard from Mrs. Redfern that Linda Marshall bought candles early in the morning on the day of the murder, and she seemed embarrassed when it was discovered what she had bought. I can clearly imagine the scene that followed. Linda made a wax effigy - perhaps adding a small bundle of Eleanor's red hair to strengthen the magic - and then pierced the heart with a needle, put it in the fireplace, placed some paper scraps and cardboard underneath, lit a fire, and melted the wax effigy.
"This behavior was childish and superstitious, but it showed one thing: the desire to kill. What if this desire was not just in her mind? Could Linda Marshall have really killed her stepmother? At first, it seemed like she had a perfect alibi - but in fact, as I pointed out earlier, the time evidence was provided by Linda herself, and she may have exaggerated the time by fifteen minutes.
"It is very likely that once Mrs. Redfern left the beach, Linda followed her and went up the mountain, crossed the narrow ridge, ran down the ladder, found her stepmother on the beach, strangled her, and climbed back up the ladder before Miss Bustle and Patrick Redfern's boat arrived. She could have gone back to the gull bay, swam, and then returned to the hotel when she felt it was appropriate."

Everything was so stable and safe, until Gordon Claude's unexpected marriage.
"Of course, dear," Adele continued, "we were all surprised. If there was one thing that seemed certain, it was that Gordon would never marry again, you know. He seemed to have many family ties and familial relationships."

"He was always so kind and friendly," Mrs. Marchmont continued, "although he could be a little domineering at times. He never liked to eat at a table that was polished to a shine, always insisting that I put down an old-fashioned tablecloth. "It's certainly to his advantage to indulge his whims," Lynn said dryly. She then asked curiously, "How did he meet his...second wife? You didn't tell me in your letter."

Lynn was silent. It was unreasonable for her not to be upset about the latest developments, but it didn't seem to fit with Gordon's own plans. Most of his property would go to his young wife, but he would surely have made provision for the rest of the family he had always urged to rely on him. He had repeatedly advised them not to save money or make plans for the future. He had told Jeremy, "You'll be a rich man when I'm gone." He often told her mother, "Don't worry, Adela. I'll take care of Lynn - you know that, and I don't want you to move out of this house - it's your home. Send me all the repair bills."
Lynn's thoughts were interrupted by Mrs. MacIntyre dramatically producing a stack of bills, her lips trembling.

"That's the correct procedure, yes," he said. "The true democratic procedure is for all those present to vote."
Sally Finch impatiently exclaimed, "What? What is it?" She said, "It's a party, all friends together. Let's hear what Mr. Poirot has to say. Let's not make a fuss over nothing."
"I couldn't agree more, Sally," said Nigel.
Poirot nodded.
"Very good," he said. "Since you all asked me, I'll answer. My suggestion is quite simple. Mrs. Haberdashers, or Mrs. Nicolaites, should call the police immediately."
Chapter 5
Poirot's suggestion was unexpected, and it was met not with a series of protests or criticisms but with an uncomfortable silence that seemed to settle over the room.
While the air was momentarily frozen, Poirot was escorted to Mrs. Haberdashers' sitting room by the hostess. Before leaving, he simply said a polite goodbye – "Goodnight everyone."
Mrs. Haberdashers switched on the lights, closed the door, and invited Poirot to sit in a chair by the fireplace. The pleasant, welcoming expression on her face was replaced by suspicion and anxiety. She offered him a cigarette, but Poirot politely declined, explaining that he preferred his own. He also offered her one, but she declined, saying in a distracted manner, "I don't smoke, Mr. Poirot."
She sat down opposite him, hesitated for a moment, and then said, "I believe you are right, M. Poirot. Perhaps we should call the police about this, especially after the malicious ink incident. But I would rather you hadn't said it so directly."
"Ah," said Poirot, lighting a small cigarette and watching the smoke rise. "You mean I should have been more discreet?"

"Alright, what did we get? Not much. But I want to tell you something, Cobbs. I'll be back tomorrow with a search warrant. We'll say everything is normal when we leave, so they'll think it's over. However, something is still going on here. Tomorrow, I'll search the place from top to bottom. When you don't know what you're looking for, it's the hardest, but we still have a chance to find something that could give us a clue. The girl who just left was quite interesting, she was very self-assured, and I strongly suspect she knows something."

Hercule Poirot was going through his correspondence when he stopped midway through dictating a sentence. Miss Lemon looked up at him in surprise.
"What is it, M. Poirot?"
"I was daydreaming! Anyway, this letter isn't important. Miss Lemon, please give your sister a call. I need to speak with her."
"Yes, Poirot."
Soon, Poirot strode out of the room and took the telephone receiver from his secretary's hand.
"Hello!" he said.
"Hello, is this Poirot?"
Mrs. Hubbard was out of breath.
"Mrs. Haberdashere, I hope I'm not disturbing you?"
"I've been disturbed all day," Mrs. Haberdashere said.
"Is there a problem?" Poirot asked delicately.
"Mr. Poirot, you said it all. They did it. Inspector Sharp questioned all the students yesterday, and today he came back with a search warrant. And I've been dealing with Mrs. Nicoletti, who's gone quite mad."
Poirot expressed some sympathy.
"I just have a small question to ask. You gave me a list of missing items and other strange occurrences. I want to know if these are listed in chronological order?"
"What do you mean?"
"I mean, are these things listed in the order they were lost?"
"No, not really. I'm sorry, I just wrote down whatever came to mind. I apologize for misleading you."

"This is a truly awful thing, Miss Pema," he said, "and I'm afraid it's quite a shock to you. I need to get a clear understanding of the whole incident from you. I know -" he glanced quickly at the police report he had been given, "Hilary Webb was the one who actually found the body. Miss Pema, if you allow me to use your kitchen, I would like to bring Miss Webb there and speak with her privately."
He opened the door connecting the dining room and the kitchen, waiting for the girl to enter. A young plainclothes detective was already in the kitchen, sitting at a table with a Formica-topped surface, writing something quietly.
"This chair looks quite comfortable," Hakcastle said, pulling a modern-style Windsor chair.
Hilary Webber sat nervously, her big fearful eyes staring straight at him.
Hakcastle almost said, "Dear, I won't eat you," but he held back and said instead,
"Don't worry. We just want to know what happened. Your name is Hilary Webber. Your address?"
"14 Palmerston Road, a little further down the gas works."
"Okay, next. I assume you have a job?"
"Yes, I'm a stenographer typist, and I work at Miss Martin's Document Printing Agency."
"Cavendish Document Printing Agency, is that the full name?"
"Yes."
"How long have you been working there?"
"About a year. Well, to be exact, ten months."
"Okay. Now tell me, how did you end up at 19 Wilbraham Crescent today?"
"Well, it's like this. Miss Pember called the typewriting agency and asked for a stenographer to come here at 3 pm. So when I came back from lunch, Miss Martin sent me here."
"Is that just a regular shift, or do you guys arrange these kinds of jobs differently?"
"Actually, it's not exactly like that. Miss Pember specifically asked for me to come."

"When Miss Weaver entered the living room," continued Huckleberry, "she found a dead man lying on the floor."
Miss Martin was shocked and speechless for a while.
"You mean 'a dead man', detective?"
"A murdered man," said Huckleberry. "To be precise, a stabbed man."
"Oh, dear," said Miss Martin. "This child must be devastated."
It seemed that Miss Martindale was the type of person who spoke conservatively and modestly.
"Is there any connection between you and this Mr. R. H. Corey, Miss Martindale?"
"I don't think so, no."
"Working at a small-town insurance company?"
Miss Martindale still shook her head.
"You should realize that I'm in a dilemma," the detective said. "You said Miss Pemmeru called you and asked Miss Sheila Webber to come to her house at three o'clock, but Miss Pemmeru denied it. Miss Sheila Webber went there and then found a dead body. " He waited expectantly.
Miss Martindale looked at him blankly.
"It's impossible for all this to happen to me," she expressed disbelief.
Dick Hackett sighed and stood up.
"This is quite good," he said politely. "You've been running the company for a while, haven't you?"
"Yes, fifteen years. The company has grown well, starting small and expanding only when we had enough staff. I now employ eight girls who are always busy."
"You must have written a lot of literature," Hakaste said, looking up at the photos on the wall.

"Are you Inspector Hackett?" she asked. "Miss Martin is waiting for you."
She led him into the inner office, where Miss Martin immediately began to berate him.
"This is simply disgraceful, Inspector Hackett, absolutely disgraceful! You must get to the bottom of this, you must get to the bottom of it immediately! Stop dilly-dallying! It's the police's duty to protect the public, and that's exactly what we need now. Protection. I want my girls to be protected, and we urgently need protection!"
"Certainly, Miss Martin, that—"
"Are you going to deny that my two girls are victims? It's obvious, someone irresponsible, with some kind of, well, what they call these days, a perverted psychology, targets shorthand typists or typewriting agencies. They deliberately torture them. First, Miss Webber was cruelly teased, sent to discover a corpse, something that might drive a nervous girl insane. Now this has happened. A girl so innocent and kind was murdered in a telephone booth. You must investigate thoroughly, Inspector."
"What I want to do most now is to get to the bottom of this, Miss Martindeer. I came to see if you could give me some help."
"Help! What help can I give you? If I could help, I would have found you by now! You must find out who killed this poor girl, Iena, and who played this cruel trick on Miss Hila. I have high standards for my girls, Inspector, I expect them to be diligent and not be late or disheveled. But I cannot tolerate them being killed or involved in murder. I want to protect them, and I want to see the people paid by the state protect them so they can work in peace. She glared at him, looking like a furious tigress.
"Give us some time, Miss Martindeer." he said.

chunk_context.text:
The sign formed a T; the intersection formed a T; and a T-shaped mark was hastily drawn on the door of the victim's house, not far from the intersection. It was a crazy idea to form a T with a person.
The local police were at a loss. Van was eccentric but a quiet, harmless man. He had no enemies and no friends. His only friend was a simple man named Clinton, who had been playing the role of Van's servant. Clinton had disappeared, and according to the evidence that was not made public, the district attorney, Crummett of Hampshire County, believed that this servant was another victim of the bloodthirsty maniac who had written a chapter in the modern American crime chronicle.
There were more similar reports, including details of the unfortunate principal's rural life in Arroyo, bits of information gathered by the police about Van and Clinton's last known whereabouts, and the district attorney's exaggerated announcement.
Ellery took off his glasses, wiped them, and put them back on, scanning the terrible relics left at the scene with sharp eyes.
Near the top of the signpost's arms, there were many small holes left by the police who had dug out the nails. Each hole was surrounded by an irregular rust-brown stain, and thin brown streaks slowly seeped out of the hole, which were the blood that had flowed from the victim's injured hands. There were two more holes on the signpost's arms that extended out, with edges that were not clearly visible, left by the nails that had been driven in to support the body in the armpits. The entire signpost was covered in dried blood, forming a crisscross pattern, very dirty. This blood flowed down from the victim's neck, which was cracked near the top of the signpost.

Bernheim made a gurgling sound in his throat. "Oh, yes, Clinton is very strong. He can lift a whole barrel of sugar! But he wouldn't harm a fly, coroner, I remember once... "
"All right, Mr. Stapleton," he said impatiently. "Mayor Hollis, please come to the witness stand again."
Matt Hollis's face lit up, and Elyot decided he was a slick little man.
"Are you the head of the town council, Mayor Hollis?"
"Yes!"
"Tell the jury everything you know about Andrew Vance."
"He was always satisfactory, kept to himself, a hard-working fellow. After school he lived in the nice little house I rented him, some people thought he had been robbed, others that he was a foreigner, but I didn't think so. The mayor spoke briefly, "Quiet, that's all there is to it. No trouble with neighbors? Well, that's his business. If he didn't want to go fishing with me and Constable Redden, that was his business. Mayor Hollar smiled and nodded. "Besides, he spoke perfect English, just like you and me, Mr. Coroner."
"Did you know of any visitors who came to see him?"
"No, of course I can't be sure. But he was an odd character," the mayor continued thoughtfully, "a few times I went to Pittsburgh on business and he asked me to buy him some books – strange books, things to make him look the part. Philosophical, historical, about the stars, and so on."
"Yes, yes, very interesting, Mr. Hollar. By the way, you're the banker of Arroyo, aren't you?"
"Yes, I am." The mayor blushes, lowering his eyes modestly. Ellery deduces from his expression that he holds sway over the town of Arroyo.
"Did Andrew Van have an account with you at the bank?"

chunk_context.text:
At the northern end of the Kyoto Basin lies a place called "Kama," and further north is Mount Danwa, which directly pierces the Sea of Japan. The residence of the Miura family is located there. The natural scenery, untouched by the hustle and bustle of the times, spreads out in all directions, with countless sights to behold. If one were to seek to retire and become a hermit, this place would be the most suitable.
However, from a geographical perspective, it is only a one and a half hour drive from the city, and there is not much difference from the suburban new residential areas. Some company employees now spend two or three hours commuting, so this place might be a decent location. The environment is also favored by nature, and the land prices are particularly cheap.
After a while, we arrived at a bright place. The previously unruly branches were neatly trimmed, indicating that we had entered the territory of the Matsuzaki family.
There was a building resembling a door in front of us. The door was in a half-collapsed state, with a Kama-style iron gun tip pointing upwards, forming an ellipse, a rare structure in Japan. The paint had peeled off, and it seemed that the owner had no intention of repairing it.
After passing through the door, we walked along a 500-meter-long tree-lined avenue. The trees, which are often seen in French films with only their tops covered in leaves, seemed to have been neglected and were half withered and weak.
I slowed down in the tree-lined avenue and drove slowly.
"That's it," said Kumagai, pointing with his hand.
The sandy road ended at a small arc at the fountain in the distance, and our destination, the Inkyou Castle, loomed in front of us.
The Inkyou Castle had a dark overall tone, resembling a giant old man squatting there.

"It's possible. In 1919, when Medvedev stayed in the city of Sparrow, the assassination of the Tsar family was widely reported both domestically and internationally. At that time, the vast fortune of the world's richest family, the Romanovs, disappeared, and only Medvedev knew about it. It would have been easy to kill him and take the fortune for themselves.
"And this time period coincides with the rapid growth of the company, which is quite interesting."
"But what does this have to do with Kumagai-san?"
The inspector seemed to sense that McCarto was changing the subject and urged him to continue.
"So, did the one who wrote his own requiem, Medvedev, have any descendants?"
"According to my investigation, he had a woman in Japan who was like a mistress. When Medvedev's body was found, she was already pregnant. She has not been heard from since then, and the child she carried should now be around seventy years old. In other words, does Medvedev have any grandsons or great-grandchildren?"
"You're saying that Kumagai-san is?"
"It's possible. If he believed his great-grandfather was killed by the Inagaki family, if he turned into a devil and swore revenge at the grave of his great-grandfather, to wipe out the Inagaki family."
"Is he really Medvedev's great-grandson?" Detective Jouji clenched his fists and leaned forward to ask.
McArthur shrugged: "This is where you come in to investigate. I was just giving an example. Of course, this is the most reliable scenario."
McArthur leaned back in his chair, as if announcing that everything was over. The sense of exhaustion even infected me.
"That's all I have to say."
With these words, McArthur's thirty-minute speech came to an end, accompanied by a tragic, legendary conclusion.
No one spoke a word.
The unexpected conclusion left everyone speechless. It was not a conclusion that could be believed just because it was said.
However, no one could offer an effective rebuttal.

chunk_context.text:
Poirot did not believe that the woman known as Eleanor Steward would ever want to be alone in her life. A man like Hercule Poirot, who had seen so much, knew it at once. How could it be otherwise? Eleanor Marshall was clearly meeting someone, and Poirot knew very well who that person would be – at least he thought he did.
However, he soon realized that he was wrong on this point. Just after the raft had rounded the headland and disappeared, Patrick Redfern and Kenneth Marshall emerged from the hotel and walked down the beach together.
Marshall nodded to Poirot. "Good morning, Poirot. Have you seen my wife?"
Poirot replied evasively, "Is she up so early?"
Marshall said, "She's not in her room." He looked up at the sky. "It's a beautiful day, I should go swimming now. I have a lot to do this morning."
Patrick Redfern, meanwhile, scanned the beach. He sat down next to Poirot, waiting for his intended. Poirot asked, "Where is your wife, Redfern? Is she up early too?"
Patrick Redfern said, "Christine? Oh, she's gone out painting. She's been quite taken with art lately." He spoke with an air of impatience, clearly distracted. As time passed, he grew increasingly agitated, clearly waiting for Eleanor to appear. He turned at the sound of footsteps, hoping it was Eleanor emerging from the hotel.
He was disappointed time and again. First came the Gardners with their knitting and books, followed by Miss Bustle. Mrs. Gardner continued her industrious work, sitting down in her chair and immediately starting to knit while she chatted nonstop.
"Poirot sir, it seems unusually quiet on the beach this morning. Where has everyone gone?"
Poirot replied that the families with children had gone out to sea in their boats, likely to spend the day there.
"Ah, that explains the quiet. Only one person is swimming this morning, Mr. Marshall."

"However, as I have said before, I soon encountered an insurmountable obstacle. Patrick Redfern could not have killed her because he was with us on the beach first, and then with Miss Bustle on the ship before the body was discovered. So I had to take a different approach to thinking. There are several other possibilities, such as her husband - with the help of Miss Darnley - because they were both lying about something suspicious. She could have been silenced because she accidentally stumbled upon a smuggler. It could also have been done by a religious fanatic. Alternatively, it could have been her stepdaughter. This last point once led me to believe it was the truth. Linda's attitude during her first police interrogation was suspicious. Later, when I spoke to her again, it further convinced me that Linda thought she was guilty."
"Are you saying that she believed herself to have actually killed Elena just because she imagined it?" asked Rosamond in a tone of disbelief.

Indeed, they all relied on Gordon Claude. This did not mean that any family member was a parasite or idle. Jeremy Claude was a senior partner in a law firm, and Lionel Claude was a practicing physician.
However, behind the routine work and ordinary days, there was a solid financial cushion that made people feel comfortable. There was never a need for thrift or saving. The future was secure. Gordon Claude, a widower without children, would take care of everything. He had told everyone, and not just once, that it was a done deal.
His widowed sister, Adela Marchmont, might have moved into a smaller, more manageable house, but she stayed in the White House. Lin En attended elite schools. She had the opportunity to accept any expensive training she desired, thanks to the regular checks from her Gordon uncle.
Everything was so stable and safe, until Gordon Claude's unexpected marriage.
"Of course, dear," Adele continued, "we were all surprised. If there was one thing that seemed certain, it was that Gordon would never marry again, you know. He seemed to have many family ties and familial relationships."
Yes, Lynn thought, there were already enough relatives. Perhaps sometimes it would feel a little too much?
"He was always so kind and friendly," Mrs. Marchmont continued, "although he could be a little domineering at times. He never liked to eat at a table that was polished to a shine, always insisting that I put down an old-fashioned tablecloth. In fact, he even sent me a most beautiful Venetian lace tablecloth from Italy."
"It's certainly to his advantage to indulge his whims," Lynn said dryly. She then asked curiously, "How did he meet his...second wife? You didn't tell me in your letter."

Lynn was silent. It was unreasonable for her not to be upset about the latest developments, but it didn't seem to fit with Gordon's own plans. Most of his property would go to his young wife, but he would surely have made provision for the rest of the family he had always urged to rely on him. He had repeatedly advised them not to save money or make plans for the future. He had told Jeremy, "You'll be a rich man when I'm gone." He often told her mother, "Don't worry, Adela. I'll take care of Lynn - you know that, and I don't want you to move out of this house - it's your home. Send me all the repair bills."
Lynn's thoughts were interrupted by Mrs. MacIntyre dramatically producing a stack of bills, her lips trembling.
"Look at all these," she sighed. "What am I going to do? What am I going to do, Lynn? The bank manager wrote to me this morning saying I was overdrawn. I don't know how I got overdrawn. I've been so careful. But it seems my investments haven't been as profitable as they used to be. He said the taxes have gone up. And all these yellow slips - war damage insurance - you have to pay them whether you like it or not."
Lynn glanced at the bills. There were no extravagant expenses listed. They showed only the replacement of slate tiles on the roof, repairs to the fence, the replacement of the old water heater in the kitchen - and a new main water pipe. But they added up to a considerable sum.

chunk_context.text:
Thus, it was not until July 1st, eight days after Inspector Vane received a telegram from Megalas, that the Helen approached the Long Island coast. Port authorities made arrangements for it to quickly pass through New York Harbor. The Helen, after a brief delay, was accompanied by a police boat and several small vessels as it entered Long Island Sound. These small vessels were hired by ambitious reporters who found it difficult to leave the Helen's deck, which had been polished with a grindstone [1].
Eight days... Eight days of calm and uneventful sailing. Even the funeral was a calm affair. Brad was buried in a rather unimpressive cemetery on Long Island, or rather, in an unsuitable environment. The press noticed that Mrs. Brad displayed remarkable fortitude in bearing this severe test. Even her daughter, who had no blood ties to the deceased, displayed more grief at the funeral than the widow herself.
The search for Werger Croscak was expanded into a nationwide manhunt. His physical description was sent to all police departments and county sheriffs' offices across the United States, as well as to all port officials; he was under surveillance by police in all forty-eight states, Canada, and Mexico. Despite the large net, no blackfish was caught; the man disappeared without a trace, as if he had flown into the sky from the ground. There was no trace of Clinton either.

"I considered the possibility of Brad, but discarded it immediately: Brad's body had been confirmed by his widow, and there was a berry-shaped mole on the dead man's thigh. And for the same logical reasons, I also considered whether it could have been Meagal: no, it was impossible, as Temple had diagnosed Meagal's illness as a particular hernia, and Rumson had found the same type of hernia on the corpse hanging from the mast of the Helen. So, Brad and Meagal's bodies were indeed themselves. After excluding the extremely small possibility of a completely unknown person being involved, there were only two left – Wilga Crocass and Van's servant,
Ellery stopped to take a breath and continued, "Could the corpse be Croscot? Impossible. If it was Croscot, Van would not have gone to such great lengths to set up a deception; he could simply claim self-defense! He could have called the police, pointed out the corpse, and that would have been it. Given the background of the case, he would undoubtedly have been released. From Van's perspective, if he was innocent, that procedure was inevitable. And the fact that he did not do so proves that he could not do so. Why? Because the corpse was not Croscot's!
"If the corpse was not Croscot, it must be Clinton, the only remaining possibility. But Clinton was believed to have been killed in the murder case at the Arojo intersection seven months ago! Oh, but how did we know that the first corpse was Clinton? It was Van himself who said so, and he has now been proven to be the killer and a liar. We have every reason to believe that any statement Van makes that has not been verified is worth doubting. In this case, the facts point to the only possibility: the last corpse must have been Clinton's."

relation.subject: MacArthur

evidence.quote: "In the end, he could only be the second-best detective in Japan."
"I was just giving an example. Of course, this is the most reliable scenario."

relation.why_cross_chunk: Connects MacArthur's self-positioning as leading detective with his later authoritative scenario-building.

verifier.reason: MacArthur gestures he is first, calling Mutsu second-best; later he asserts most reliable scenario.

chunk_context.text:
"Ah, it's you, Mr. Kouzuki."
MacArthur seemed to notice me only just then, turning around. He should have recognized me much earlier, before we even passed each other.
MacArthur's expression told me that he had everything under control. He probably knew all the details of the incident from the police chief.
"I heard that Mutsu-tsan has run away. Running away at the last minute isn't very honorable, is it?"
"..." I remained silent.
As I had expected.
I ignored MacArthur's words and was about to take a step forward when he challenged me with a provocative tone, "In the end, he could only be the second-best detective in Japan."
"Who's the first?" I couldn't help but ask.
MacArthur whistled in response to my question, then clicked his tongue twice. He shook his head and raised his hat brim with his index finger. Then, he pointed his thumb at himself.
"Quite confident, aren't you?"
"Yes, it's only natural for Wakimura-san to be second in line after all the trouble he's been through."
It seems this person isn't even listening to what I'm saying.
"By the way, Mr. MacCarty, what's going on? Your client doesn't seem to exist anymore."
I tried to be sarcastic, but it seems he didn't even notice the subtle meaning in the words.
"The same goes for you, doesn't it? I've already talked to Kanou-san."
"Kanou-san…?" I ask incredulously. Kanou-san…
However, it was Muto who abandoned his client and betrayed him by hiding in the mountains. Kanou-san is probably just grabbing at straws now.
"What are your plans, Hagimori-san?"
The "straw" dressed in fancy clothes points the tip of his cane at me.
Caught off guard, I could only nod. But there was more to my reason for staying here. I had to fulfill my promise to Mr. Kaneda and accompany Yuki to the lakeside.
I tried to hide my emotions, but it seemed too late.

"It's possible. In 1919, when Medvedev stayed in the city of Sparrow, the assassination of the Tsar family was widely reported both domestically and internationally. At that time, the vast fortune of the world's richest family, the Romanovs, disappeared, and only Medvedev knew about it. It would have been easy to kill him and take the fortune for themselves.
"And this time period coincides with the rapid growth of the company, which is quite interesting."
"But what does this have to do with Kumagai-san?"
The inspector seemed to sense that McCarto was changing the subject and urged him to continue.
"So, did the one who wrote his own requiem, Medvedev, have any descendants?"
"According to my investigation, he had a woman in Japan who was like a mistress. When Medvedev's body was found, she was already pregnant. She has not been heard from since then, and the child she carried should now be around seventy years old. In other words, does Medvedev have any grandsons or great-grandchildren?"
"You're saying that Kumagai-san is?"
"It's possible. If he believed his great-grandfather was killed by the Inagaki family, if he turned into a devil and swore revenge at the grave of his great-grandfather, to wipe out the Inagaki family."
"Is he really Medvedev's great-grandson?" Detective Jouji clenched his fists and leaned forward to ask.
McArthur shrugged: "This is where you come in to investigate. I was just giving an example. Of course, this is the most reliable scenario."
McArthur leaned back in his chair, as if announcing that everything was over. The sense of exhaustion even infected me.
"That's all I have to say."
With these words, McArthur's thirty-minute speech came to an end, accompanied by a tragic, legendary conclusion.
No one spoke a word.
The unexpected conclusion left everyone speechless. It was not a conclusion that could be believed just because it was said.
However, no one could offer an effective rebuttal.

chunk_context.text:
Poirot did not believe that the woman known as Eleanor Steward would ever want to be alone in her life. A man like Hercule Poirot, who had seen so much, knew it at once. How could it be otherwise? Eleanor Marshall was clearly meeting someone, and Poirot knew very well who that person would be – at least he thought he did.
However, he soon realized that he was wrong on this point. Just after the raft had rounded the headland and disappeared, Patrick Redfern and Kenneth Marshall emerged from the hotel and walked down the beach together.
Marshall nodded to Poirot. "Good morning, Poirot. Have you seen my wife?"
Poirot replied evasively, "Is she up so early?"
Marshall said, "She's not in her room." He looked up at the sky. "It's a beautiful day, I should go swimming now. I have a lot to do this morning."
Patrick Redfern, meanwhile, scanned the beach. He sat down next to Poirot, waiting for his intended. Poirot asked, "Where is your wife, Redfern? Is she up early too?"
Patrick Redfern said, "Christine? Oh, she's gone out painting. She's been quite taken with art lately." He spoke with an air of impatience, clearly distracted. As time passed, he grew increasingly agitated, clearly waiting for Eleanor to appear. He turned at the sound of footsteps, hoping it was Eleanor emerging from the hotel.
He was disappointed time and again. First came the Gardners with their knitting and books, followed by Miss Bustle. Mrs. Gardner continued her industrious work, sitting down in her chair and immediately starting to knit while she chatted nonstop.
"Poirot sir, it seems unusually quiet on the beach this morning. Where has everyone gone?"
Poirot replied that the families with children had gone out to sea in their boats, likely to spend the day there.
"Ah, that explains the quiet. Only one person is swimming this morning, Mr. Marshall."

"However, as I have said before, I soon encountered an insurmountable obstacle. Patrick Redfern could not have killed her because he was with us on the beach first, and then with Miss Bustle on the ship before the body was discovered. So I had to take a different approach to thinking. There are several other possibilities, such as her husband - with the help of Miss Darnley - because they were both lying about something suspicious. She could have been silenced because she accidentally stumbled upon a smuggler. It could also have been done by a religious fanatic. Alternatively, it could have been her stepdaughter. This last point once led me to believe it was the truth. Linda's attitude during her first police interrogation was suspicious. Later, when I spoke to her again, it further convinced me that Linda thought she was guilty."
"Are you saying that she believed herself to have actually killed Elena just because she imagined it?" asked Rosamond in a tone of disbelief.

chunk_context.text:
Lynn was silent. It was unreasonable for her not to be upset about the latest developments, but it didn't seem to fit with Gordon's own plans. Most of his property would go to his young wife, but he would surely have made provision for the rest of the family he had always urged to rely on him. He had repeatedly advised them not to save money or make plans for the future. He had told Jeremy, "You'll be a rich man when I'm gone." He often told her mother, "Don't worry, Adela. I'll take care of Lynn - you know that, and I don't want you to move out of this house - it's your home. Send me all the repair bills."
Lynn's thoughts were interrupted by Mrs. MacIntyre dramatically producing a stack of bills, her lips trembling.
"Look at all these," she sighed. "What am I going to do? What am I going to do, Lynn? The bank manager wrote to me this morning saying I was overdrawn. I don't know how I got overdrawn. I've been so careful. But it seems my investments haven't been as profitable as they used to be. He said the taxes have gone up. And all these yellow slips - war damage insurance - you have to pay them whether you like it or not."
Lynn glanced at the bills. There were no extravagant expenses listed. They showed only the replacement of slate tiles on the roof, repairs to the fence, the replacement of the old water heater in the kitchen - and a new main water pipe. But they added up to a considerable sum.
Mrs. Marchmont lamented:

Indeed, they all relied on Gordon Claude. This did not mean that any family member was a parasite or idle. Jeremy Claude was a senior partner in a law firm, and Lionel Claude was a practicing physician.
However, behind the routine work and ordinary days, there was a solid financial cushion that made people feel comfortable. There was never a need for thrift or saving. The future was secure. Gordon Claude, a widower without children, would take care of everything. He had told everyone, and not just once, that it was a done deal.
His widowed sister, Adela Marchmont, might have moved into a smaller, more manageable house, but she stayed in the White House. Lin En attended elite schools. She had the opportunity to accept any expensive training she desired, thanks to the regular checks from her Gordon uncle.
Everything was so stable and safe, until Gordon Claude's unexpected marriage.
"Of course, dear," Adele continued, "we were all surprised. If there was one thing that seemed certain, it was that Gordon would never marry again, you know. He seemed to have many family ties and familial relationships."
Yes, Lynn thought, there were already enough relatives. Perhaps sometimes it would feel a little too much?
"He was always so kind and friendly," Mrs. Marchmont continued, "although he could be a little domineering at times. He never liked to eat at a table that was polished to a shine, always insisting that I put down an old-fashioned tablecloth. In fact, he even sent me a most beautiful Venetian lace tablecloth from Italy."
"It's certainly to his advantage to indulge his whims," Lynn said dryly. She then asked curiously, "How did he meet his...second wife? You didn't tell me in your letter."

Sharp asked a few more questions, but Lenn Bates could not provide any further information. Next, Sharp was to see Valerie Hobhouse.
Valerie was calm, poised, and slightly on edge. She was far less tense than the two men who had spoken before her. She said she liked Celia. Celia was not very bright, and the way she had expressed her feelings for Colin McNaughton was quite pitiful.

Valerie shrugged.
"You mean to attract that self-important idiot Colin?"
"You're quick on the uptake, Miss Hobhouse. Yes, that's exactly what I mean. I don't suppose you suggested it, did you?"
Valerie looked amused.
"Oh, dear sir, I wouldn't want my favorite scarf to be torn into shreds. I'm not that selfless."

I know -" he glanced quickly at the police report he had been given, "Hilary Webb was the one who actually found the body. Miss Pema, if you allow me to use your kitchen, I would like to bring Miss Webb there and speak with her privately."
He opened the door connecting the dining room and the kitchen, waiting for the girl to enter. A young plainclothes detective was already in the kitchen, sitting at a table with a Formica-topped surface, writing something quietly.
"This chair looks quite comfortable," Hakcastle said, pulling a modern-style Windsor chair.
Hilary Webber sat nervously, her big fearful eyes staring straight at him.
Hakcastle almost said, "Dear, I won't eat you," but he held back and said instead,
"Don't worry. We just want to know what happened. Your name is Hilary Webber. Your address?"
"14 Palmerston Road, a little further down the gas works."
"Okay, next. I assume you have a job?"
"Yes, I'm a stenographer typist, and I work at Miss Martin's Document Printing Agency."
"Cavendish Document Printing Agency, is that the full name?"
"Yes."
"How long have you been working there?"
"About a year. Well, to be exact, ten months."
"Okay. Now tell me, how did you end up at 19 Wilbraham Crescent today?"
"Well, it's like this. Miss Pember called the typewriting agency and asked for a stenographer to come here at 3 pm. So when I came back from lunch, Miss Martin sent me here."
"Is that just a regular shift, or do you guys arrange these kinds of jobs differently?"
"Actually, it's not exactly like that. Miss Pember specifically asked for me to come."

"When Miss Weaver entered the living room," continued Huckleberry, "she found a dead man lying on the floor."
Miss Martin was shocked and speechless for a while.
"You mean 'a dead man', detective?"
"A murdered man," said Huckleberry. "To be precise, a stabbed man."
"Oh, dear," said Miss Martin. "This child must be devastated."
It seemed that Miss Martindale was the type of person who spoke conservatively and modestly.
"Is there any connection between you and this Mr. R. H. Corey, Miss Martindale?"
"I don't think so, no."
"Working at a small-town insurance company?"
Miss Martindale still shook her head.
"You should realize that I'm in a dilemma," the detective said. "You said Miss Pemmeru called you and asked Miss Sheila Webber to come to her house at three o'clock, but Miss Pemmeru denied it. Miss Sheila Webber went there and then found a dead body. " He waited expectantly.
Miss Martindale looked at him blankly.
"It's impossible for all this to happen to me," she expressed disbelief.
Dick Hackett sighed and stood up.
"This is quite good," he said politely. "You've been running the company for a while, haven't you?"
"Yes, fifteen years. The company has grown well, starting small and expanding only when we had enough staff. I now employ eight girls who are always busy."
"You must have written a lot of literature," Hakaste said, looking up at the photos on the wall.

Good news! Mrs. Brand finally confessed! She admitted to everything! She said it was all her sister and her husband who orchestrated it. She thought they just wanted "to knock him out so he couldn't tell the difference between the real Mrs. Brand and the fake one!" This seems plausible! I think she wasn't the mastermind behind it all.
The people at the Pólo Market confirmed that Miss Martin is the "American" woman who bought the two clocks they mentioned.
Mrs. McNeil just said she saw Dugan sitting in Mr. Brand's truck when it went into the garage. Is that true?
My friend, Colin, married the girl. I suppose you'll ask me if he's crazy? Best wishes to you.

Richard Huckleberry

chunk_context.text:
Thus, it was not until July 1st, eight days after Inspector Vane received a telegram from Megalas, that the Helen approached the Long Island coast. Port authorities made arrangements for it to quickly pass through New York Harbor. The Helen, after a brief delay, was accompanied by a police boat and several small vessels as it entered Long Island Sound. These small vessels were hired by ambitious reporters who found it difficult to leave the Helen's deck, which had been polished with a grindstone [1].
Eight days... Eight days of calm and uneventful sailing. Even the funeral was a calm affair. Brad was buried in a rather unimpressive cemetery on Long Island, or rather, in an unsuitable environment. The press noticed that Mrs. Brad displayed remarkable fortitude in bearing this severe test. Even her daughter, who had no blood ties to the deceased, displayed more grief at the funeral than the widow herself.
The search for Werger Croscak was expanded into a nationwide manhunt. His physical description was sent to all police departments and county sheriffs' offices across the United States, as well as to all port officials; he was under surveillance by police in all forty-eight states, Canada, and Mexico. Despite the large net, no blackfish was caught; the man disappeared without a trace, as if he had flown into the sky from the ground. There was no trace of Clinton either.

"I considered the possibility of Brad, but discarded it immediately: Brad's body had been confirmed by his widow, and there was a berry-shaped mole on the dead man's thigh. And for the same logical reasons, I also considered whether it could have been Meagal: no, it was impossible, as Temple had diagnosed Meagal's illness as a particular hernia, and Rumson had found the same type of hernia on the corpse hanging from the mast of the Helen. So, Brad and Meagal's bodies were indeed themselves. After excluding the extremely small possibility of a completely unknown person being involved, there were only two left – Wilga Crocass and Van's servant,
Ellery stopped to take a breath and continued, "Could the corpse be Croscot? Impossible. If it was Croscot, Van would not have gone to such great lengths to set up a deception; he could simply claim self-defense! He could have called the police, pointed out the corpse, and that would have been it. Given the background of the case, he would undoubtedly have been released. From Van's perspective, if he was innocent, that procedure was inevitable. And the fact that he did not do so proves that he could not do so. Why? Because the corpse was not Croscot's!
"If the corpse was not Croscot, it must be Clinton, the only remaining possibility. But Clinton was believed to have been killed in the murder case at the Arojo intersection seven months ago! Oh, but how did we know that the first corpse was Clinton? It was Van himself who said so, and he has now been proven to be the killer and a liar. We have every reason to believe that any statement Van makes that has not been verified is worth doubting. In this case, the facts point to the only possibility: the last corpse must have been Clinton's."

I ignored MacArthur's words and was about to take a step forward when he challenged me with a provocative tone, "In the end, he could only be the second-best detective in Japan."
"Who's the first?" I couldn't help but ask.
MacArthur whistled in response to my question, then clicked his tongue twice. He shook his head and raised his hat brim with his index finger. Then, he pointed his thumb at himself.
"Quite confident, aren't you?"
"Yes, it's only natural for Wakimura-san to be second in line after all the trouble he's been through."
It seems this person isn't even listening to what I'm saying.
"By the way, Mr. MacCarty, what's going on? Your client doesn't seem to exist anymore."
I tried to be sarcastic, but it seems he didn't even notice the subtle meaning in the words.
"The same goes for you, doesn't it? I've already talked to Kanou-san."
"Kanou-san…?" I ask incredulously. Kanou-san…
However, it was Muto who abandoned his client and betrayed him by hiding in the mountains. Kanou-san is probably just grabbing at straws now.
"What are your plans, Hagimori-san?"
The "straw" dressed in fancy clothes points the tip of his cane at me.
Caught off guard, I could only nod. But there was more to my reason for staying here. I had to fulfill my promise to Mr. Kaneda and accompany Yuki to the lakeside.
I tried to hide my emotions, but it seemed too late.

"It's possible. In 1919, when Medvedev stayed in the city of Sparrow, the assassination of the Tsar family was widely reported both domestically and internationally. At that time, the vast fortune of the world's richest family, the Romanovs, disappeared, and only Medvedev knew about it. It would have been easy to kill him and take the fortune for themselves.
"And this time period coincides with the rapid growth of the company, which is quite interesting."
"But what does this have to do with Kumagai-san?"
The inspector seemed to sense that McCarto was changing the subject and urged him to continue.
"So, did the one who wrote his own requiem, Medvedev, have any descendants?"
"According to my investigation, he had a woman in Japan who was like a mistress. When Medvedev's body was found, she was already pregnant. She has not been heard from since then, and the child she carried should now be around seventy years old. In other words, does Medvedev have any grandsons or great-grandchildren?"
"You're saying that Kumagai-san is?"
"It's possible. If he believed his great-grandfather was killed by the Inagaki family, if he turned into a devil and swore revenge at the grave of his great-grandfather, to wipe out the Inagaki family."
"Is he really Medvedev's great-grandson?" Detective Jouji clenched his fists and leaned forward to ask.
McArthur shrugged: "This is where you come in to investigate. I was just giving an example. Of course, this is the most reliable scenario."
McArthur leaned back in his chair, as if announcing that everything was over. The sense of exhaustion even infected me.
"That's all I have to say."
With these words, McArthur's thirty-minute speech came to an end, accompanied by a tragic, legendary conclusion.
No one spoke a word.
The unexpected conclusion left everyone speechless. It was not a conclusion that could be believed just because it was said.
However, no one could offer an effective rebuttal.

chunk_context.text:
Poirot did not believe that the woman known as Eleanor Steward would ever want to be alone in her life. A man like Hercule Poirot, who had seen so much, knew it at once. How could it be otherwise? Eleanor Marshall was clearly meeting someone, and Poirot knew very well who that person would be – at least he thought he did.
However, he soon realized that he was wrong on this point. Just after the raft had rounded the headland and disappeared, Patrick Redfern and Kenneth Marshall emerged from the hotel and walked down the beach together.
Marshall nodded to Poirot. "Good morning, Poirot. Have you seen my wife?"
Poirot replied evasively, "Is she up so early?"
Marshall said, "She's not in her room." He looked up at the sky. "It's a beautiful day, I should go swimming now. I have a lot to do this morning."
Patrick Redfern, meanwhile, scanned the beach. He sat down next to Poirot, waiting for his intended. Poirot asked, "Where is your wife, Redfern? Is she up early too?"
Patrick Redfern said, "Christine? Oh, she's gone out painting. She's been quite taken with art lately." He spoke with an air of impatience, clearly distracted. As time passed, he grew increasingly agitated, clearly waiting for Eleanor to appear. He turned at the sound of footsteps, hoping it was Eleanor emerging from the hotel.
He was disappointed time and again. First came the Gardners with their knitting and books, followed by Miss Bustle. Mrs. Gardner continued her industrious work, sitting down in her chair and immediately starting to knit while she chatted nonstop.
"Poirot sir, it seems unusually quiet on the beach this morning. Where has everyone gone?"
Poirot replied that the families with children had gone out to sea in their boats, likely to spend the day there.
"Ah, that explains the quiet. Only one person is swimming this morning, Mr. Marshall."

"However, as I have said before, I soon encountered an insurmountable obstacle. Patrick Redfern could not have killed her because he was with us on the beach first, and then with Miss Bustle on the ship before the body was discovered. So I had to take a different approach to thinking. There are several other possibilities, such as her husband - with the help of Miss Darnley - because they were both lying about something suspicious. She could have been silenced because she accidentally stumbled upon a smuggler. It could also have been done by a religious fanatic. Alternatively, it could have been her stepdaughter. This last point once led me to believe it was the truth. Linda's attitude during her first police interrogation was suspicious. Later, when I spoke to her again, it further convinced me that Linda thought she was guilty."
"Are you saying that she believed herself to have actually killed Elena just because she imagined it?" asked Rosamond in a tone of disbelief.

Sitting in an inconspicuous spot was another little man, looking like a foreigner with black handlebar mustache. The Kloes were all there: Mr. and Mrs. Jeremy Kloes, Mr. and Mrs. Leonel Kloes, Mr. Rolly Kloes, Mrs. Marchmont, and Lynn - all accounted for. Major Porter sat alone, looking worried. I just managed to make my bed look rumpled and have breakfast with Rosemary. I never thought the police would suspect her."
"Of course, I had no idea who killed him! I couldn't imagine anyone who would want to kill him. As far as I know, besides myself and Rosalind, there was no one with a motive to kill."
"This," said Poirot, "has always been a tricky puzzle. Motive. You and your sister had a motive to kill Jardine, and every member of the de Clercy family had a motive to kill your sister."
David exclaimed:

"No. It was a well-thought-out, premeditated crime. One of the packets of bromide sleeping powder was switched for morphine – the one at the bottom of the box."

She would look across the table, in her usual way, and say: 'I'm afraid the facts don't bear out, statistically they're quite conclusive...' and so on. That's a criticism, you know, especially of someone who speaks without thinking, like Nigel Chapman."
"Ah, Nigel Chapman."
"And it was green ink."
"So you think Nigel did it?"
"Well, it's possible. He's a bit of a grudge-holder, you know, and I think he might have a bit of a racial thing going on. Probably the only one of us with that."
"Can you remember anyone else who has been annoyed by Miss Johnson's habit of correcting people?”
"Well, Colin McNaughton has been a bit put out by her from time to time, and there have been one or two occasions when she's got Gene Thompson riled up.”
Sharp asked a few more questions, but Lenn Bates could not provide any further information. Next, Sharp was to see Valerie Hobhouse.
Valerie was calm, poised, and slightly on edge. She was far less tense than the two men who had spoken before her. She said she liked Celia. Celia was not very bright, and the way she had expressed her feelings for Colin McNaughton was quite pitiful.
"Do you think she's someone who would steal, Miss Hobhouse?”
"Oh, I suppose so. I don't really know much about that."
"Do you think anyone has advised her for her actions?"
Valerie shrugged.
"You mean to attract that self-important idiot Colin?"
"You're quick on the uptake, Miss Hobhouse. Yes, that's exactly what I mean. I don't suppose you suggested it, did you?"
Valerie looked amused.
"Oh, dear sir, I wouldn't want my favorite scarf to be torn into shreds. I'm not that selfless."
"Who else do you think might have advised her to do that?"

Suddenly he sat up straight, shaking his disheveled golden hair.
"Who did it! I'll kill him! I'll kill him! The despicable murderer!"
"Calm down, Mr. Chapman. Yes, I understand your feelings. It's a terrible thing."
"Pat has never hurt anyone..."
Detective Sharp comforted him and led him out of the room, then returned to the bedroom. He leaned over the dead girl and carefully took something out from between her fingers.
2
Sweat dripped down Jeremiah's forehead as he looked from one person to another, his shocked black eyes darting around the room.
"I saw nothing, heard nothing, I swear to you, I know nothing. I was in the kitchen with Maria, making vegetable noodle soup, grating cheese..."
Detective Sharp cut him off.
"No one accuses you. We're just trying to clarify some timelines. Was anyone in or out of this house within the past hour?"
"I don't know. How am I supposed to know?"
"You can see who comes and goes from the kitchen window, can't you?"
"Maybe, yes."
"Then tell us."
"There's always someone coming and going at this time of day."
"Who was here from six o'clock to six thirty-five when we arrived?"
"Only Nigel, Mrs. Habberd, and Miss Hobhouse were not here."
"When did they leave?"
"Mrs. Habberd went out before tea, and she hasn't come back yet."
"Go on."
"Nigel left about half an hour ago, at six o'clock, looking very agitated. He just came back with you."
"That's right, yes."
"Miss Valerie left exactly at six o'clock, when the clock struck. She was dressed semi-formally and very stylish. She's still out."
"Is everyone else here?"
"Yes, sir, everyone is here."
Mr. Sharp glanced down at his notebook, which recorded the time of Mrs. Patricia's call. The exact time was 6:08.
"Is everyone else here in this house during this time? Has anyone come back?"

"This is a truly awful thing, Miss Pema," he said, "and I'm afraid it's quite a shock to you. I need to get a clear understanding of the whole incident from you. I know -" he glanced quickly at the police report he had been given, "Hilary Webb was the one who actually found the body. Miss Pema, if you allow me to use your kitchen, I would like to bring Miss Webb there and speak with her privately."
He opened the door connecting the dining room and the kitchen, waiting for the girl to enter. A young plainclothes detective was already in the kitchen, sitting at a table with a Formica-topped surface, writing something quietly.
"This chair looks quite comfortable," Hakcastle said, pulling a modern-style Windsor chair.
Hilary Webber sat nervously, her big fearful eyes staring straight at him.
Hakcastle almost said, "Dear, I won't eat you," but he held back and said instead,
"Don't worry. We just want to know what happened. Your name is Hilary Webber. Your address?"
"14 Palmerston Road, a little further down the gas works."
"Okay, next. I assume you have a job?"
"Yes, I'm a stenographer typist, and I work at Miss Martin's Document Printing Agency."
"Cavendish Document Printing Agency, is that the full name?"
"Yes."
"How long have you been working there?"
"About a year. Well, to be exact, ten months."
"Okay. Now tell me, how did you end up at 19 Wilbraham Crescent today?"
"Well, it's like this. Miss Pember called the typewriting agency and asked for a stenographer to come here at 3 pm. So when I came back from lunch, Miss Martin sent me here."
"Is that just a regular shift, or do you guys arrange these kinds of jobs differently?"
"Actually, it's not exactly like that. Miss Pember specifically asked for me to come."

"When Miss Weaver entered the living room," continued Huckleberry, "she found a dead man lying on the floor."
Miss Martin was shocked and speechless for a while.
"You mean 'a dead man', detective?"
"A murdered man," said Huckleberry. "To be precise, a stabbed man."
"Oh, dear," said Miss Martin. "This child must be devastated."
It seemed that Miss Martindale was the type of person who spoke conservatively and modestly.
"Is there any connection between you and this Mr. R. H. Corey, Miss Martindale?"
"I don't think so, no."
"Working at a small-town insurance company?"
Miss Martindale still shook her head.
"You should realize that I'm in a dilemma," the detective said. "You said Miss Pemmeru called you and asked Miss Sheila Webber to come to her house at three o'clock, but Miss Pemmeru denied it. Miss Sheila Webber went there and then found a dead body. " He waited expectantly.
Miss Martindale looked at him blankly.
"It's impossible for all this to happen to me," she expressed disbelief.
Dick Hackett sighed and stood up.
"This is quite good," he said politely. "You've been running the company for a while, haven't you?"
"Yes, fifteen years. The company has grown well, starting small and expanding only when we had enough staff. I now employ eight girls who are always busy."
"You must have written a lot of literature," Hakaste said, looking up at the photos on the wall.

"Are you Inspector Hackett?" she asked. "Miss Martin is waiting for you."
She led him into the inner office, where Miss Martin immediately began to berate him.
"This is simply disgraceful, Inspector Hackett, absolutely disgraceful! You must get to the bottom of this, you must get to the bottom of it immediately! Stop dilly-dallying! It's the police's duty to protect the public, and that's exactly what we need now. Protection. I want my girls to be protected, and we urgently need protection!"
"Certainly, Miss Martin, that—"
"Are you going to deny that my two girls are victims? It's obvious, someone irresponsible, with some kind of, well, what they call these days, a perverted psychology, targets shorthand typists or typewriting agencies. They deliberately torture them. First, Miss Webber was cruelly teased, sent to discover a corpse, something that might drive a nervous girl insane. Now this has happened. A girl so innocent and kind was murdered in a telephone booth. You must investigate thoroughly, Inspector."
"What I want to do most now is to get to the bottom of this, Miss Martindeer. I came to see if you could give me some help."
"Help! What help can I give you? If I could help, I would have found you by now! You must find out who killed this poor girl, Iena, and who played this cruel trick on Miss Hila. I have high standards for my girls, Inspector, I expect them to be diligent and not be late or disheveled. But I cannot tolerate them being killed or involved in murder. I want to protect them, and I want to see the people paid by the state protect them so they can work in peace. She glared at him, looking like a furious tigress.
"Give us some time, Miss Martindeer." he said.
