They sat down. Ellery said, "Sheriff, have you seen that crazy hillbilly, old Pete lately?”
"Old Pete? Oh, that's odd,” Rudden said, glancing slyly at Asheem, "I haven't seen him for several weeks. He doesn't come into town often, old Pete, I mean, not often; but this time - I haven't seen him for two months! Must have brought a lot of supplies down the mountain last time; you can ask Bernheim.”
"Do you know where his shack is?” Asheem asked.
"I think I know... what do you want with old Pete? Planning to arrest him? The old coot hasn't done anything wrong... no,” the sheriff hastily added as Asheem frowned, "it's none of my business... I've never been to old Pete's shack - hardly anyone has. It's in the cave area - the old folks, they're all so wise - people are a bit afraid. Old Pete's shack is in a very desolate place in the mountains, you won't find it.”
"Can you show us the way, Sheriff?” Ellery asked.
"Of course! I think I can find the place," said Redden, getting up, wagging his tail like an old, fat, well-trained dog. "You don't want the news to spread, do you?" he asked casually.
"No!" said Escham. "Don't tell your wife."
The sheriff snorted. "Don't worry about that. I don't have a wife, thank God... Amen."
He didn't take them to the street in front of the town hall where they had parked the car, but through a back door and onto a little-used street. Redden and Escham waited, and Ellery quickly circled the town hall and jumped into the Duesenberg. Two minutes later, the car was on the little street, and the three men drove away from the town hall, Redden stamping hard on the accelerator.

Chapter 1: Aroo's Christmas
The story begins at a crossroads, half a mile outside the small West Virginia village of Aroo, where one road leads from New Kensington to Pietown [1], and another leads to Aroo.
Ellery Queen immediately realized that the terrain was important. His first glance revealed many other things, but only found evidence conflicting and confusing. Everything seemed out of place, and it seemed necessary to leave the crossroads and think things over more carefully.
Ellery Queen, the erudite and cosmopolitan man, found himself standing in the cold and gloomy weather of the West Virginia handle region [2] at two o'clock in the afternoon on December 26th, next to an old Duesenberg [3] race car. This unusual phenomenon was caused by a combination of factors, with the most important being his father, Inspector Quin, who advocated working on holidays. The elderly man was deeply engrossed in his daily work, the so-called "police customs," and worked tirelessly. The crime situation in Chicago was always dire, and the police commissioner invited the top police officers from major cities to his jurisdiction to commiserate over the terrible state of affairs.
It was during the trip with his father, the Inspector, from the hotel to the Chicago Police Headquarters that Ellery learned about the perplexing case in Aroo, which was dubbed the "T-shaped murder" by the United Press. There were many elements in the report that piqued Ellery's interest - such as the fact that Andrew Van was decapitated and nailed to a cross on Christmas morning - that prompted him to pull his father out of the smoky Chicago meeting and drive off in a secondhand, fast Duesenberg towards the east.

Mrs. Gardner continued to knit her needles, "Honestly, Mr. Poirot, seeing you here has given me an idea - not that I'm not excited to see you, because I am, and Mr. Gardner knows it - but I can't help but wonder, you know, that you might be here for professional reasons. "You know, Mr. Poirot, Mrs. Gardner is very sensitive."
Hercule Poirot waved his hand in the air. "Then rest assured, madam, my purpose here is the same as yours - to relax and enjoy a holiday. I haven't thought about solving any cases."
"There are no bodies on Pirate Island," said Miss Bustle stiffly.
"Ah, that may not be the case," said Hercule Poirot, pointing to the beach below. "Look at them, lying there in rows. What do they look like? Men and women? They look like nothing but - bodies[2]!"

There are several other possibilities, such as her husband - with the help of Miss Darnley - because they were both lying about something suspicious. She could have been silenced because she accidentally stumbled upon a smuggler. It could also have been done by a religious fanatic. Alternatively, it could have been her stepdaughter. This last point once led me to believe it was the truth. Linda's attitude during her first police interrogation was suspicious. chunk_context.text:
Although she had enjoyed her time abroad, it was nice to leave the Women's Royal Naval Service and become a free woman again. The job had been interesting, with various social events and amusing, yet there were also tedious routines and the feeling of being confined with her comrades, which sometimes made her want to escape.
It was during that time that she longed for Wormsley Valley and this shabby yet cool and comfortable house, and her dear mother.
Lyn had a love-hate relationship with her mother. When she was far away from home, she loved her more, and the annoying things were put aside, and even if she remembered them, they only made her more homesick. Dear mother, she could drive you crazy! If only she didn't have to listen to her mother's voice, so sweet and melodious, but full of complaints, pronouncing the same old clichés over and over again.
She was here now, having completed her service, free, and back in White House. She had been home for three days, and an inexplicable dissatisfaction and restlessness were creeping up on her. Everything was the same - almost unchanged - the house, her mother, Rolly, the farm, and the family. The only thing that was different and shouldn't be was herself...
"Darling..." Mrs. Marchmont's delicate call came from downstairs. "Would you like me to bring a tray of breakfast to your room?"
Lynn called out loudly:
"No, thank you. I'll come down."
"Why," she thought, "mom insists on saying 'my daughter.' That's too silly!"

Indeed, they all relied on Gordon Claude. This did not mean that any family member was a parasite or idle. Jeremy Claude was a senior partner in a law firm, and Lionel Claude was a practicing physician.
However, behind the routine work and ordinary days, there was a solid financial cushion that made people feel comfortable. There was never a need for thrift or saving. The future was secure. Gordon Claude, a widower without children, would take care of everything. He had told everyone, and not just once, that it was a done deal.
His widowed sister, Adela Marchmont, might have moved into a smaller, more manageable house, but she stayed in the White House. Lin En attended elite schools. She had the opportunity to accept any expensive training she desired, thanks to the regular checks from her Gordon uncle.
Everything was so stable and safe, until Gordon Claude's unexpected marriage.
"Of course, dear," Adele continued, "we were all surprised. If there was one thing that seemed certain, it was that Gordon would never marry again, you know. He seemed to have many family ties and familial relationships."
Yes, Lynn thought, there were already enough relatives. Perhaps sometimes it would feel a little too much?
"He was always so kind and friendly," Mrs. Marchmont continued, "although he could be a little domineering at times. He never liked to eat at a table that was polished to a shine, always insisting that I put down an old-fashioned tablecloth. In fact, he even sent me a most beautiful Venetian lace tablecloth from Italy."
"It's certainly to his advantage to indulge his whims," Lynn said dryly. She then asked curiously, "How did he meet his...second wife? You didn't tell me in your letter."

Poirot's suggestion was unexpected, and it was met not with a series of protests or criticisms but with an uncomfortable silence that seemed to settle over the room.
While the air was momentarily frozen, Poirot was escorted to Mrs. Haberdashers' sitting room by the hostess. Before leaving, he simply said a polite goodbye – "Goodnight everyone."
Mrs. Haberdashers switched on the lights, closed the door, and invited Poirot to sit in a chair by the fireplace. The pleasant, welcoming expression on her face was replaced by suspicion and anxiety. She offered him a cigarette, but Poirot politely declined, explaining that he preferred his own. He also offered her one, but she declined, saying in a distracted manner, "I don't smoke, Mr. Poirot."
She sat down opposite him, hesitated for a moment, and then said, "I believe you are right, M. Poirot. Perhaps we should call the police about this, especially after the malicious ink incident. But I would rather you hadn't said it so directly."
"Ah," said Poirot, lighting a small cigarette and watching the smoke rise. "You mean I should have been more discreet?"

Chapter 1: Aroo's Christmas
The story begins at a crossroads, half a mile outside the small West Virginia village of Aroo, where one road leads from New Kensington to Pietown [1], and another leads to Aroo.
Ellery Queen immediately realized that the terrain was important. His first glance revealed many other things, but only found evidence conflicting and confusing. Everything seemed out of place, and it seemed necessary to leave the crossroads and think things over more carefully.
Ellery Queen, the erudite and cosmopolitan man, found himself standing in the cold and gloomy weather of the West Virginia handle region [2] at two o'clock in the afternoon on December 26th, next to an old Duesenberg [3] race car. This unusual phenomenon was caused by a combination of factors, with the most important being his father, Inspector Quin, who advocated working on holidays. The elderly man was deeply engrossed in his daily work, the so-called "police customs," and worked tirelessly. The crime situation in Chicago was always dire, and the police commissioner invited the top police officers from major cities to his jurisdiction to commiserate over the terrible state of affairs.
It was during the trip with his father, the Inspector, from the hotel to the Chicago Police Headquarters that Ellery learned about the perplexing case in Aroo, which was dubbed the "T-shaped murder" by the United Press. There were many elements in the report that piqued Ellery's interest - such as the fact that Andrew Van was decapitated and nailed to a cross on Christmas morning - that prompted him to pull his father out of the smoky Chicago meeting and drive off in a secondhand, fast Duesenberg towards the east.

MacArthur seemed to notice me only just then, turning around. He should have recognized me much earlier, before we even passed each other.
MacArthur's expression told me that he had everything under control. He probably knew all the details of the incident from the police chief.
"I heard that Mutsu-tsan has run away. Running away at the last minute isn't very honorable, is it?"
"..." I remained silent.
As I had expected.
I ignored MacArthur's words and was about to take a step forward when he challenged me with a provocative tone, "In the end, he could only be the second-best detective in Japan."
"Who's the first?" I couldn't help but ask.
MacArthur whistled in response to my question, then clicked his tongue twice. He shook his head and raised his hat brim with his index finger. Then, he pointed his thumb at himself.
"Quite confident, aren't you?"
"Yes, it's only natural for Wakimura-san to be second in line after all the trouble he's been through."
It seems this person isn't even listening to what I'm saying.
"By the way, Mr. MacCarty, what's going on? Your client doesn't seem to exist anymore."
I tried to be sarcastic, but it seems he didn't even notice the subtle meaning in the words.
"The same goes for you, doesn't it? I've already talked to Kanou-san."
"Kanou-san…?" I ask incredulously. Kanou-san…
However, it was Muto who abandoned his client and betrayed him by hiding in the mountains. Kanou-san is probably just grabbing at straws now.
"What are your plans, Hagimori-san?"
The "straw" dressed in fancy clothes points the tip of his cane at me.
Caught off guard, I could only nod. But there was more to my reason for staying here. I had to fulfill my promise to Mr. Kaneda and accompany Yuki to the lakeside.
I tried to hide my emotions, but it seemed too late.

"It's possible. In 1919, when Medvedev stayed in the city of Sparrow, the assassination of the Tsar family was widely reported both domestically and internationally. At that time, the vast fortune of the world's richest family, the Romanovs, disappeared, and only Medvedev knew about it. It would have been easy to kill him and take the fortune for themselves.
"And this time period coincides with the rapid growth of the company, which is quite interesting."
"But what does this have to do with Kumagai-san?"
The inspector seemed to sense that McCarto was changing the subject and urged him to continue.
"So, did the one who wrote his own requiem, Medvedev, have any descendants?"
"According to my investigation, he had a woman in Japan who was like a mistress. When Medvedev's body was found, she was already pregnant. She has not been heard from since then, and the child she carried should now be around seventy years old. In other words, does Medvedev have any grandsons or great-grandchildren?"
"You're saying that Kumagai-san is?"
"It's possible. If he believed his great-grandfather was killed by the Inagaki family, if he turned into a devil and swore revenge at the grave of his great-grandfather, to wipe out the Inagaki family."
"Is he really Medvedev's great-grandson?" Detective Jouji clenched his fists and leaned forward to ask.
McArthur shrugged: "This is where you come in to investigate. I was just giving an example. Of course, this is the most reliable scenario."
McArthur leaned back in his chair, as if announcing that everything was over. The sense of exhaustion even infected me.
"That's all I have to say."
With these words, McArthur's thirty-minute speech came to an end, accompanied by a tragic, legendary conclusion.
No one spoke a word.
The unexpected conclusion left everyone speechless. It was not a conclusion that could be believed just because it was said.
However, no one could offer an effective rebuttal.

"Ah? Yes, dear." Mr. Gardner said.
"But Mr. Kelsey assured us immediately. He said the sanitation facilities are absolutely state-of-the-art, and the food is top-notch. He was right. What I like best is that it gives you a sense of 'intimacy,' you know what I mean. In these small places, we can easily gather together and chat, and everyone is very familiar with each other.
"If there's one small flaw in the British, it's that they like to keep their distance from you until they get to know you, and they always like to coldly interact with you for a year or two before they start to be friendly, and then they're the friendliest of all. Mr. Kelsey said there are many extraordinary people here, and I think he's right. For example, Mr. Poirot, and Miss Darnley. Oh, I was so happy to find out who you are, didn't you, Odell?"
"Yes, dear," said Mr. Gardner.
"Ha!" Miss Bustard couldn't hold back any longer, "What a surprise, Mr. Poirot?"
Hercule Poirot waved his hand to object, but it was only out of politeness and did not affect Mrs. Gardner's continued rambling.
"You know, Mr. Poirot, I heard a lot about you from Miss Robson. She is... Miss Robson and I met her in May at Bardonhurst, of course, Miss Robson told us all about the case in Egypt [1], the case of the murder of Linnet Ridgeway. She said you were magnificent. I've been looking forward to meeting you, haven't I, Odell?"
"Yes, dear."

"She'll appeal to Mr. Poirot," said Miss Burrage. "She doesn't like the sun either."
Mrs. Redfern took off her rubber swimming cap and shook her hair loose. She had fair, pale hair that matched her pale complexion, and her legs and arms were also very white. Major Barry chuckled. "She looks a bit underdone compared to them, doesn't she?"
Miss Burrage said, "Miss Redfern, you've certainly won Mr. Poirot's approval. He doesn't like people who sunbathe, saying they're like meat on a butcher's block or something like that."
Christine Redfern smiled ruefully. "I wish I could sunbathe, but my skin doesn't tan, it just gets red and then I get terrible rashes all over my arms."
"At least it's better than Eileen Gardner's arms getting all hairy," said Miss Bustle. She saw Christine's questioning look and continued, "Mrs. Gardner was in high spirits this morning, her mouth never stopped. 'Isn't it, Odell?' 'Yes, dear.'” She paused and then said, "But, Mr. Poirot, why don't you play a little joke on her? Why not tell her that you're here to investigate a terrible murder, that the killer is a psychopath and has been confirmed to be staying in this hotel?"
Hercule Poirot sighed. "I'm afraid she would believe me."
Colonel Barry chuckled. "She would believe you."
Emily Bustle said, "I don't think even someone like Mrs. Gardner would believe there would be a murder here. This isn't the kind of place where bodies turn up."
"Why not, Miss?" Hercule Poirot countered. "Why wouldn't there be a body on a pirate island, the place you call 'dead'?"
"I don't know why, but I just feel that some places are less likely to have a murder than others, and this isn't one of those places…" She trailed off, unable to find the right words to express her thoughts.

"She certainly was, old chap. I don't doubt it for a moment. Any judge would say the same. She wouldn't be blamed for it."
"Judge?" David asked alertly.
The other man's response seemed apologetic:
"I was thinking of bigamy."
"What do you want?" David was furious.
"Don't get so worked up, buddy. We're just trying to brainstorm, see what's best – in other words, what's best for your sister. Nobody wants to be known as a bad guy. André – well, André has always been a chivalrous guy."
"Now?" David asked sharply.
"Me. I said it."
"You're saying Robert André is still alive. Where is he?"
Yatton leaned forward—his voice lowered to a whisper.
"Do you really want to know, Hunter? It's better if you don't. As you and Rosaline know, André Haas died in Africa. That's good, and even if he's still alive, he doesn't know his wife has remarried, and he's none the wiser. Of course, if he did know, he would have come looking for her by now… you see, Rosaline inherited a lot of money from her second husband—well, of course, she didn't have the right to use it… André is a man who cares a lot about honor. He wouldn't like her to inherit the property through deceit."
"What do you mean by 'not so well'?"
Yatton shook his head solemnly.
"His health is deteriorating. He needs medical attention—special treatment—unfortunately, it's quite expensive."
The last two words slipped from his mouth with a hint of finality, as if it was all meant to be. And that was exactly what David Hunter had been waiting for, without realizing it.
"Expensive?" he said.
"Yes — unfortunately, everything costs money. André is a poor man, this poor man is actually broke."
For a moment, David glanced around the room with his eyes. He noticed the backpack hanging on the chair. There were no suitcases in sight.

"Hunter and his sister. They're beaten – out. Rosalind won't get Gordon's money. We will. Gordon's will still stands, and since she wasn't married to him when her first husband was alive, she can't claim it. I'll get a quarter of it. Understand?"
"You – you're sure about all this?"
He stared at her, a slight confusion on his face for the first time.
"Of course I'm sure! It's elementary. Now everything is resolved. Just as Gordon planned. Everything is just as it was, as if those two never came in to interfere."
Everything is just as it was... but Lynn thought, you can't erase what has already happened. You can't pretend those things never occurred. She spoke slowly:
"What about them?"
"Ah?" She knew Rowley hadn't considered this yet, "I don't know. I guess they go back where they came from. You know, I think —" she could see him slowly putting his thoughts together, "Yes, I think we should do something for her. I mean, she genuinely married Gordon. I think she really believed her first husband was dead. It wasn't her fault. Yes, we must do something for her — give her a decent living allowance. Split it among us all."
"You like her, don't you?" Linh said.
"Well, yes," he pondered, "in a way, I do like her. She's a good girl, can recognize a cow right away."
"I can't," Linh said.
"Oh, you'll learn," Rolle said kindly.
"What about David?" Linh asked.
Rolly's face darkened.
"Let David go to hell! The money was never his anyway. He just came here to eat his sister's soft food."
"No, Rolly, it's not like that—not at all. He's… He's an adventurer, maybe—"
"And a damn murderer!"
She breathed a sigh.
"What do you mean?"
"Well, who do you think killed André?"
She exclaimed:
"I don't believe it! I don't believe it!"

"You're not troubling me at all. It's I who am intrigued. But while I think, I can start from a practical angle. A starting point...the shoes, those evening shoes...yes, we can start there. Miss Lemon!"
"What is it, M. Poirot?" Miss Lemon withdrew her thoughts from the filing and sat up straighter, reaching for a notepad and pencil.
"Perhaps Mrs. Hubbard will give you the other shoe. Then you go to the lost property office at Baker Street Station. When did you realize it was missing?"
Mrs. Hubbard thought for a moment.
"Oh, I can't remember the exact time, Mr. Poirot. Maybe two months ago. I can't remember a more precise time, but I can deduce it from Sally Fench's dinner party."
"Alright, um... " He turned his head back to Miss Lemon. "You should write it vaguely. You could say you left a shoe on the Circle Line, which is the most likely place, or on another train. Or maybe on a bus. How many bus routes are there around Mountbatten Street?"
"Only two, Mr. Poirot."
"Excellent. If Baker Street is a dead end, try Scotland Yard. Tell them it was lost in a taxi."
"Go to Lambeth Police Station (note: Poirot referred to Scotland Yard as a nickname for the London Police Force, while Miss Lemon specified the exact district)."
Poirot waved his hand.
"You always know so much about these things."
"But why do you think—" Mrs. Hubbard was about to ask, but Poirot interrupted her.
"Let's see what comes of it first. Then, no matter what the result is, Mrs. Harbottle, the two of us must discuss further. At that time, you must tell me everything I need to know."
"I think I've told you everything I know."

"Alright, what did we get? Not much. But I want to tell you something, Cobbs. I'll be back tomorrow with a search warrant. We'll say everything is normal when we leave, so they'll think it's over. However, something is still going on here. Tomorrow, I'll search the place from top to bottom. When you don't know what you're looking for, it's the hardest, but we still have a chance to find something that could give us a clue. The girl who just left was quite interesting, she was very self-assured, and I strongly suspect she knows something."

Hercule Poirot was going through his correspondence when he stopped midway through dictating a sentence. Miss Lemon looked up at him in surprise.
"What is it, M. Poirot?"
"I was daydreaming! Anyway, this letter isn't important. Miss Lemon, please give your sister a call. I need to speak with her."
"Yes, Poirot."
Soon, Poirot strode out of the room and took the telephone receiver from his secretary's hand.
"Hello!" he said.
"Hello, is this Poirot?"
Mrs. Hubbard was out of breath.
"Mrs. Haberdashere, I hope I'm not disturbing you?"
"I've been disturbed all day," Mrs. Haberdashere said.
"Is there a problem?" Poirot asked delicately.
"Mr. Poirot, you said it all. They did it. Inspector Sharp questioned all the students yesterday, and today he came back with a search warrant. And I've been dealing with Mrs. Nicoletti, who's gone quite mad."
Poirot expressed some sympathy.
"I just have a small question to ask. You gave me a list of missing items and other strange occurrences. I want to know if these are listed in chronological order?"
"What do you mean?"
"I mean, are these things listed in the order they were lost?"
"No, not really. I'm sorry, I just wrote down whatever came to mind. I apologize for misleading you."

"I squatted down. I felt a man's hand. It was cold and there was no pulse… I got up and walked over here, sat down and waited for someone to come. It won't be long, someone will come. That young woman, whoever she is, will call for help. I think it's best not to leave this house."
I was shocked by the woman's calmness. She didn't scream or panic in the house, she just sat there quietly waiting. She was rational, but we still had to take action.
She questioned:
"Who are you?"
"My name is Colin Lamb. I just happened to pass by."
"Where did the young girl go?"
"I let her rest near the entrance. She was scared. Where is the nearest place to call for help?"
"Follow this path for about fifty yards, and there's a phone booth just before the corner."
"Yes, I remember passing by there. I'm going to call the police. You—" I hesitated.
I didn't know whether to say "Are you going to stay here?" or "Are you okay?"
She spared me the decision.
"You should bring the girl inside," she said firmly.
"I don't know if she'll come," I said skeptically.
"Of course, don't let her come into this room. Tell her to wait in the dining room next to the entrance. Tell her I'm brewing tea for her."
She approached me.
"But can you do that?" she asked.
A slight smirk appeared on her face.
"My dear young man, since I moved into this house fourteen years ago, I have been cooking in the kitchen myself. Being blind doesn't mean I'm useless."
"I'm sorry, I was too ignorant. Perhaps I can ask for your name?"
"Millee Pema-Chhoe – Miss."
I left the room and walked out along the path. The girl saw me and struggled to get up.
"I, I think I'm almost better now."
I helped her stand up, smiling,

I handed him some photographs taken by the police.
"Who is this?" Colonel Beck asked.
"The deceased."
"It sounds preposterous to me that it was the girl you were so infatuated with who killed him."
"You haven't heard the story yet," I said, "I haven't told you."
"I don't need to be told," Colonel Beck flicked his cigar. "Go ahead and attend your trial, my boy, watch out for that girl. Is her name Diana, or Artemis, or any name like the crescent moon?"
"No, not at all."
"Oh, remember, it might be!"

Chapter 14
Narrative by Colin Lamb
I haven't been to Whitehall House for a long time. A few years ago, it was a grand modern apartment building. Now, there are many impressive and more modern-looking buildings on both sides of the street. Going inside, I found that the building has recently been renovated. The walls have been repainted in light yellow or light green.
I took the elevator upstairs and rang the doorbell at room 203. The door was opened by a polite male servant named George. He greeted me with a welcoming smile.
"Mr. Colin! It's been a while since I've seen you."
"Yes, you're doing well, George?"
"I'm doing well, thank you, sir."
I lowered my voice. "How is he?"
George also lowered his voice, although it seemed unnecessary, as he had been speaking carefully from the beginning.
"I think, sir, that his mood is a bit low."
I sympathetically nodded.
"This way, sir -" He took my hat.
"Please announce me as Mr. Colin Lamb, sir."
"Certainly, sir." He opened the door and called out in a clear voice. "Mr. Colin Lamb to see you, sir."
He stepped back, allowing me to pass, and I entered the room.

"I thought you weren't interested," Ellery said, jumping off the sidewalk. "Hey, come here!" he called to a country bumpkin wrapped in a blue work suit, sweeping the sidewalk with a worn-out broom. "Is the sheriff of Arroyo here?" The man stared at him in disbelief. "Of course, it's written on the sign… come on, you crook."
It was a dreary residential area with few buildings. The Duesenberg stopped in front of a building whose skeletal structure was made of shoddy wood, like a box for growing mushrooms in the past. Next to it was a general store with an old gas pump in front, and then a car repair shop. A handwritten sign hung proudly in front of the mushroom box-shaped building: Arroyo Village Hall. They found the gentleman they were looking for sitting at a desk at the back of the building, asleep. The sign on the door read "Town Marshal."
Quinlan snorted, and the town marshal lifted his heavy eyelids, scratched his head, and said in a hoarse whisper, "If you're looking for Matt Hollis, he's out."
Ellery smiled. "We're looking for Arroyo's Sheriff Redden."
"Oh, I am," he said. "What do you want?"
"Sheriff," Ellery said menacingly, "allow me to introduce Richard Quin, the head of the New York Police Department's Homicide Division—he's here in person."
"Who?" The sheriff stared blankly, "New York?"
"Absolutely," Ellery said, stepping on his father's toes, "Now, Sheriff, we want—"
"Sit," said Sheriff Luddon, kicking a chair over to Quin. Quin grunted and sat down elegantly. "This Mr. Van's business, huh? I don't see how the New Yorkers would be interested. What's going on?"
Ellery took out a cigarette case and offered it to the sheriff, who grumbled and stuffed a large wad of chewing tobacco into his mouth.
"Tell me everything, Sheriff."

Although District Attorney Escham had eaten, they had wasted valuable time. Ellery was inexplicably excited, fidgeting with his food; although he looked tired, his eyes were bright and shone with some unspoken thoughts.
At a few minutes to five, the Duesenberg stopped in front of a building where the prominent figures of Arroyo were. They got out of the car, their joints cracking. Escham stretched his arms wide, ignoring the curious eyes of a fat German old man - Bernheim, the respected owner of Arroyo's grocery store - and a country bumpkin dressed in blue denim, who seemed to be sweeping the sidewalk in front of the town hall all year round. Escham yawned and said, "Well, let's get it done quickly. Where is the county sheriff, Mr. Queen?"
Ellery led the way into the back of the house, where the sheriff's office was located. He knocked on the door, and a gravelly male voice said, "Come in, you son of a bitch!"
They went inside. Sheriff Rudden sat there, his massive body drenched in sweat, as if he hadn't moved since Ellery's last visit six months ago. As he opened his mouth, his fangs protruded from his fat, red face.
[1661] "If it isn't Mr. Quin," Redden yelled, putting his big feet down with a bang, "I'm a son of a bitch! Come in, come in. Still chasing the guy who killed our principal?"
"Still on the case, Sheriff," Ellery smiled. "Meet the man who upholds the law. This is New York County District Attorney Escham. Sheriff Redden - Escham, sir."
Escham grumbled, not extending his hand. The sheriff grinned. "We had some bigwigs come to our town last year, sir, so don't be so arrogant."
Escham gasped in surprise. "You heard what I said... what do you care about, Mr. Quin?"
Ellery quickly said, "Can we sit down? We've been driving for a long time."

At the front of the porch stood a man in a marble arch. It was he who called out to us - Detective Tsubaki. Detective Tsubaki was wearing a trench coat, his only decent piece of clothing. He spread his hands wide, showing surprise. Detective Tsubaki was already forty, but he had a childlike face when he smiled.
Detective Tsubaki was a rare person who was straightforward in his emotions. Of course, when dealing with cases, he would put on a serious face, but otherwise, he was a likable neighborhood uncle figure. It was all thanks to Detective Tsubaki's influence that a commoner like Mutsu was able to thrive in the police force.
"Detective Joujiroku, it's been a while." Mukae takes off his hat and nods slightly.
"I haven't seen you since the arson case. It's been three and a half months."

The two look at each other, as if celebrating their long-awaited reunion.
"Well, Detective Joujiroku from the investigation department has arrived, so it must be a murder case."
"You're as informed as ever, almost like a walking encyclopedia. I don't recall telling you about this..."

At that moment, I noticed a bunch of question marks spinning around in my head, as if something was ringing alarm bells in the back of my mind. However, these were just questions, similar to the things that appeared in my mind when I met the mist yesterday.
The root cause is probably Wakatsuki.

Mukai's pupils cool down: "You seem to have a sense of inferiority, which is not like you. However, I'm not yet certain that I'm the sage. Because, in fact, I was manipulated by the murderer."
"So, she's the murderer?"
"Well, there's only an eight-eighth probability at this stage. No, no, it's not good to chat with you like this. You have a great mission. You can say it's fate."

Could it be...

We continued our journey back through the fallen leaves.
White crows danced in the sky, and black crows fell to the ground.
Just as we opened the entrance gate.

Yatton leaned forward—his voice lowered to a whisper.

"What do you mean by 'not so well'?"
Yatton shook his head solemnly.
"His health is deteriorating. He needs medical attention—special treatment—unfortunately, it's quite expensive."
The last two words slipped from his mouth with a hint of finality, as if it was all meant to be. And that was exactly what David Hunter had been waiting for, without realizing it.

"What is it, M. Poirot?" Miss Lemon withdrew her thoughts from the filing and sat up straighter, reaching for a notepad and pencil.
"Perhaps Mrs. Hubbard will give you the other shoe. Then you go to the lost property office at Baker Street Station. When did you realize it was missing?"
Mrs. Hubbard thought for a moment.
"Oh, I can't remember the exact time, Mr. Poirot. Maybe two months ago. I can't remember a more precise time, but I can deduce it from Sally Fench's dinner party."
"Alright, um... " He turned his head back to Miss Lemon. "You should write it vaguely. You could say you left a shoe on the Circle Line, which is the most likely place, or on another train. Or maybe on a bus. How many bus routes are there around Mountbatten Street?"
"Only two, Mr. Poirot."
"Excellent. If Baker Street is a dead end, try Scotland Yard. Tell them it was lost in a taxi."
"Go to Lambeth Police Station (note: Poirot referred to Scotland Yard as a nickname for the London Police Force, while Miss Lemon specified the exact district)."
Poirot waved his hand.
"You always know so much about these things."
"But why do you think—" Mrs. Hubbard was about to ask, but Poirot interrupted her.
"Let's see what comes of it first. Then, no matter what the result is, Mrs. Harbottle, the two of us must discuss further. At that time, you must tell me everything I need to know."
"I think I've told you everything I know."

Mr. Archibald Bletchley nodded solemnly at his own reflection in the mirror.

Sally Finch impatiently exclaimed, "What? What is it?" She said, "It's a party, all friends together. Let's hear what Mr. Poirot has to say. Let's not make a fuss over nothing."
"I couldn't agree more, Sally," said Nigel.

"Very good," he said. "Since you all asked me, I'll answer. My suggestion is quite simple. Mrs. Haberdashers, or Mrs. Nicolaites, should call the police immediately."

While the air was momentarily frozen, Poirot was escorted to Mrs. Haberdashers' sitting room by the hostess. Before leaving, he simply said a polite goodbye – "Goodnight everyone."
Mrs. Haberdashers switched on the lights, closed the door, and invited Poirot to sit in a chair by the fireplace. The pleasant, welcoming expression on her face was replaced by suspicion and anxiety. She offered him a cigarette, but Poirot politely declined, explaining that he preferred his own. He also offered her one, but she declined, saying in a distracted manner, "I don't smoke, Mr. Poirot."
She sat down opposite him, hesitated for a moment, and then said, "I believe you are right, M. Poirot. Perhaps we should call the police about this, especially after the malicious ink incident. But I would rather you hadn't said it so directly."
"Ah," said Poirot, lighting a small cigarette and watching the smoke rise. "You mean I should have been more discreet?"

chunk_context.text:
"I thought you weren't interested," Ellery said, jumping off the sidewalk. "Hey, come here!" he called to a country bumpkin wrapped in a blue work suit, sweeping the sidewalk with a worn-out broom. "Is the sheriff of Arroyo here?" The man stared at him in disbelief. "Of course, it's written on the sign… come on, you crook."
It was a dreary residential area with few buildings. The Duesenberg stopped in front of a building whose skeletal structure was made of shoddy wood, like a box for growing mushrooms in the past. Next to it was a general store with an old gas pump in front, and then a car repair shop. A handwritten sign hung proudly in front of the mushroom box-shaped building: Arroyo Village Hall. They found the gentleman they were looking for sitting at a desk at the back of the building, asleep. The sign on the door read "Town Marshal."
Quinlan snorted, and the town marshal lifted his heavy eyelids, scratched his head, and said in a hoarse whisper, "If you're looking for Matt Hollis, he's out."
Ellery smiled. "We're looking for Arroyo's Sheriff Redden."
"Oh, I am," he said. "What do you want?"
"Sheriff," Ellery said menacingly, "allow me to introduce Richard Quin, the head of the New York Police Department's Homicide Division—he's here in person."
"Who?" The sheriff stared blankly, "New York?"
"Absolutely," Ellery said, stepping on his father's toes, "Now, Sheriff, we want—"
"Sit," said Sheriff Luddon, kicking a chair over to Quin. Quin grunted and sat down elegantly. "This Mr. Van's business, huh? I don't see how the New Yorkers would be interested. What's going on?"
Ellery took out a cigarette case and offered it to the sheriff, who grumbled and stuffed a large wad of chewing tobacco into his mouth.
"Tell me everything, Sheriff."

"Yes. Matt – he's our mayor, you know – Matt and I, we took four boys with us in a car. A mess, he – I mean, Van. I've never seen anything like it, and it's still Christmas. I call it blasphemy. As for Van, he's an atheist."
"Huh?" the officer asked quickly, his red nose poking out from the folds of the scarf, "Atheist? What does that mean?"
"Oh, maybe not an atheist," Sheriff Redden mumbled uneasily, "I'm not a regular churchgoer myself, but Van never goes. The parish priest – well, I'd better not talk about that."
"Quite extraordinary," Ellery turned to his father and said. "Indeed, it's quite extraordinary. Dad, it's like something a religious fanatic would do."
"Yes, they all say so," Judge Redden said. "I—I don't know. I'm just a country judge, you know? This jail hasn't held a vagrant in three years. But I dare say, gentlemen, it's not just about religion."
"I don't think anyone in town would be a suspect," Ellery frowned and asserted.
"Nobody would be so crazy, I tell you, it must be someone connected to Range's past."
"Has there been any strangers in town lately?"
"None... So Matt and I, and the boys, checked the height, build, clothing, and credentials of the body, and then identified him, and put the body down. On the way back to the village, we stopped at Van's house -"
"Well," Ellery said eagerly, "What did you find?"
"It was like hell," Sheriff Redden said, chewing on his tobacco, "There were signs of a violent struggle, chairs were overturned, almost everything had blood on it. The door had a big T painted in blood, as the newspaper said, and poor old Clark disappeared without a trace."
"Ah," said the officer, "Is that the servant who just walked away, huh? Did he take his clothes?"

The worst scenario was unfolding in my mind, but if it weren't, Mutsu's appearance would have no meaning. I walked towards the mansion with a complicated mood.
"Oh, it's Mutsu-san! And Hoshimo-san is here too!"
At the front of the porch stood a man in a marble arch. It was he who called out to us - Detective Tsubaki. Detective Tsubaki was wearing a trench coat, his only decent piece of clothing. He spread his hands wide, showing surprise. Detective Tsubaki was already forty, but he had a childlike face when he smiled.
Detective Tsubaki was a rare person who was straightforward in his emotions. Of course, when dealing with cases, he would put on a serious face, but otherwise, he was a likable neighborhood uncle figure. It was all thanks to Detective Tsubaki's influence that a commoner like Mutsu was able to thrive in the police force.
"Detective Joujiroku, it's been a while." Mukae takes off his hat and nods slightly.
"I haven't seen you since the arson case. It's been three and a half months."
"That's right."
The two look at each other, as if celebrating their long-awaited reunion.
"Well, Detective Joujiroku from the investigation department has arrived, so it must be a murder case."
"You're as informed as ever, almost like a walking encyclopedia. I don't recall telling you about this..."
Detective Jiro spoke while observing Shizuku's face, smiling but with a sharp gaze.

"He came for that purpose."
I smiled encouragingly at her. Although this was a bad habit of making promises for others, I didn't care about that now.
"He's like a god."
Misty, influenced by me, also smiled. Her expression was reminiscent of the smile of a water lily.
"He is a god, at least for now."
"You trust him a lot."
"Of course I do," she replied.
After saying that, I noticed the desolate look on her face.
"You can trust him too," I said more firmly.
"Trust Mr. Mukai?" she asked.
"Trust Mr. Mukai, trust the god, it doesn't matter. Only trust can bring redemption."
"The saying 'faith saves' may sound clichéd, but it's mostly true. Whether it actually exists or not is no longer the issue."
"I also believe in God. But…"
"But?"
"Ah, never mind."
Mistuho made a clumsy smile, as if to refuse any further "intrusion."
"Then I'll take my leave."
I put my robe on her shoulders and leave.
Can I really save her?
Her thoughts are no different from those of martyrs.
"Good job!"
Unbeknownst to me, Mukae had already made his way to the entrance of the courtyard. As I approached him, he clapped me on the shoulder with a loud "thump."
"You have quite the gentlemanly demeanor."
Mukae wore a smirk of low-class mischief, having witnessed the previous scene. I didn't think he meant to mock me, but I still felt embarrassed.
"The situation doesn't look good. I feel like she's on the brink of death."
As the saying goes, "Disease is born of the heart," and it's true. Even the autonomic nervous system eventually yields to willpower.
"Perhaps. But it's inevitable."
Muto surprisingly agreed, then narrowed his eyes to look at Fujiko. Fujiko seemed to be engrossed in reading a book again. The world that had conversed with me once more returned to a still image.
"What do you mean?"

Everything was so stable and safe, until Gordon Claude's unexpected marriage.
"Of course, dear," Adele continued, "we were all surprised. If there was one thing that seemed certain, it was that Gordon would never marry again, you know. He seemed to have many family ties and familial relationships."

"He was always so kind and friendly," Mrs. Marchmont continued, "although he could be a little domineering at times. He never liked to eat at a table that was polished to a shine, always insisting that I put down an old-fashioned tablecloth. Lynn was silent. It was unreasonable for her not to be upset about the latest developments, but it didn't seem to fit with Gordon's own plans. Most of his property would go to his young wife, but he would surely have made provision for the rest of the family he had always urged to rely on him. He had repeatedly advised them not to save money or make plans for the future. He had told Jeremy, "You'll be a rich man when I'm gone." He often told her mother, "Don't worry, Adela. Chapter 1
Hercule Poirot frowned.
"Miss Lemon," he called.
"What is it, M. Poirot?" she asked.
"There are three mistakes in this letter."
His voice held a note of puzzlement, for Miss Lemon, a woman who could be described as efficient to the point of being terrifying, had never made a mistake. She had never been ill, never tired, never been perturbed, and never made a mistake. In fact, she was not a woman but a machine—a perfect secretary. She knew everything and could handle all matters. She took care of M. Poirot's mundane affairs so that he could function like a machine. For years, rules and methods had been the mantra of Hercule Poirot. He had a perfect servant, George, and a perfect secretary, Miss Lemon, and rules and methods were supreme in his life. Since crispbreads could be baked in both square and round shapes, he had nothing to complain about.
Yet this morning, Miss Lemon had made three mistakes in a very simple letter, and she hadn't even noticed them. This breaking of the pattern was like the stars standing still in their orbits!
M. Poirot handed over the offending document. He was not angry, merely puzzled. It was an impossible thing—and yet it had happened!
Miss Lemon took the letter and looked at it. This was the first time M. Poirot had ever seen her blush; an expression of embarrassment, out of character for her, spread from her face to her thick, somewhat silvered hair.
"Oh dear," she said, "I can't imagine how this could have happened. But I suppose it's because of my sister."
"Your sister?"

"Alright, what did we get? Not much. But I want to tell you something, Cobbs. I'll be back tomorrow with a search warrant. We'll say everything is normal when we leave, so they'll think it's over. However, something is still going on here. Tomorrow, I'll search the place from top to bottom. When you don't know what you're looking for, it's the hardest, but we still have a chance to find something that could give us a clue. The girl who just left was quite interesting, she was very self-assured, and I strongly suspect she knows something."
Chapter 12

Hercule Poirot was going through his correspondence when he stopped midway through dictating a sentence. Miss Lemon looked up at him in surprise.
"What is it, M. Poirot?"
"I was daydreaming! Anyway, this letter isn't important. Miss Lemon, please give your sister a call. I need to speak with her."
"Yes, Poirot."
Soon, Poirot strode out of the room and took the telephone receiver from his secretary's hand.
"Hello!" he said.
"Hello, is this Poirot?"
Mrs. Hubbard was out of breath.
"Mrs. Haberdashere, I hope I'm not disturbing you?"
"I've been disturbed all day," Mrs. Haberdashere said.
"Is there a problem?" Poirot asked delicately.
"Mr. Poirot, you said it all. They did it. Inspector Sharp questioned all the students yesterday, and today he came back with a search warrant. And I've been dealing with Mrs. Nicoletti, who's gone quite mad."
Poirot expressed some sympathy.
"I just have a small question to ask. You gave me a list of missing items and other strange occurrences. I want to know if these are listed in chronological order?"
"What do you mean?"
"I mean, are these things listed in the order they were lost?"
"No, not really. I'm sorry, I just wrote down whatever came to mind. I apologize for misleading you."

At the northern end of the Kyoto Basin lies a place called "Kama," and further north is Mount Danwa, which directly pierces the Sea of Japan. The residence of the Miura family is located there. The natural scenery, untouched by the hustle and bustle of the times, spreads out in all directions, with countless sights to behold. If one were to seek to retire and become a hermit, this place would be the most suitable.
However, from a geographical perspective, it is only a one and a half hour drive from the city, and there is not much difference from the suburban new residential areas. Some company employees now spend two or three hours commuting, so this place might be a decent location. The environment is also favored by nature, and the land prices are particularly cheap.
After a while, we arrived at a bright place. The previously unruly branches were neatly trimmed, indicating that we had entered the territory of the Matsuzaki family.
There was a building resembling a door in front of us. The door was in a half-collapsed state, with a Kama-style iron gun tip pointing upwards, forming an ellipse, a rare structure in Japan. The paint had peeled off, and it seemed that the owner had no intention of repairing it.
After passing through the door, we walked along a 500-meter-long tree-lined avenue. The trees, which are often seen in French films with only their tops covered in leaves, seemed to have been neglected and were half withered and weak.
I slowed down in the tree-lined avenue and drove slowly.
"That's it," said Kumagai, pointing with his hand.
The sandy road ended at a small arc at the fountain in the distance, and our destination, the Inkyou Castle, loomed in front of us.

Captain Barry followed his gaze and saw a man of about forty years old. He had a head of beautiful hair, a slightly tanned complexion, a calm and pleasant face, and was sitting on the beach smoking a pipe and reading a Time magazine.
"Ah, that's the husband," Captain Barry said. "The fellow, Marshall."
Hercule Poirot said, "I know."
Captain Barry chuckled. As a bachelor, he had only three views of "husbands" - "obstacle," "inconvenience," and "bodyguard." He said, "He seems like a nice guy, quiet. I wonder if my Time magazine has arrived yet." He stood up and walked towards the hotel.
Poirot's gaze slowly turned to Stephen Lane's face. Stephen Lane was watching Elena Marshall and Patrick Redfern. He suddenly turned his head towards Poirot, his eyes flashing with passion. He said, "That woman is the very incarnation of evil. Do you still have any doubts?"
Poirot said slowly, "It's hard to say."
Stephen Lennard said, "But isn't it obvious? There's evil all around you."
Hercule Poirot slowly nodded.

[1] refers to "Murder on the Nile."
[2] In English, both "body" and "corpse" can be used to refer to a dead person.
[3] Patrick's nickname.
Chapter 2
As Rosamund Darnley walked over and sat down next to him, Hercule Poirot couldn't hide his joy. He had always admitted that he had a great admiration for Rosamund Darnley, just as he did for other outstanding women. He admired her exceptional beauty, her graceful posture, and her confident demeanor. He liked her smooth, jet-black hair and her carefree smile. She wore a navy blue suit with white accents, which appeared simple but was actually exquisitely tailored. Rosamund Darnley's Rosamond Darnley & Co. is one of London's most famous women's clothing companies.
She said, "I don't think I like this place, and I don't understand why I'm here."
"You've been here before, haven't you?"

About an hour later, Hercule Poirot walked along the path leading to the beach at Swan Bay, where a person sat at the end, short in stature, wearing a red shirt and deep yellow shorts. Poirot left the path and made his way to the beach, his new fashionable shoes carefully chosen for their footing. Linda Marshall turned sharply, and he thought she seemed to shrink back. He sat down beside her on the beach, her gaze falling on his face, as if a small, suspicious, and wary animal. He suddenly felt her so young and vulnerable.
She said, "What? What do you want?"
Hercule Poirot remained silent for a few minutes before saying, "You told the police commissioner that you liked your stepmother, and she was nice to you."
"So what?"
"It's not like that, is it, Miss?"
"How not?"
Poirot said, "She may not have intentionally treated you badly—I agree. But you don't like her—ah, I can see you really dislike her."
Linda said, "Perhaps I don't particularly like her, but she's dead now, and it's not seemly to say so."
Poirot sighed. "Is that the kind of education you received at school?"
"Almost, yes."
"When someone is murdered, telling the truth is more important than being polite," said Hercule Poirot.
"I knew you would say that," said Linda.
"I will say that, and I have said it. It's my duty, you know, to find out who killed Elena Marshall."
Linda muttered, "I wish I could forget about it. It's too terrible."
Poirot spoke gently. "But you can't, can you?"
Linda said, "I think a ruthless madman killed her."
Hercule Poirot whispered, "I don't think so. I don't think so."
Linda drew in a sharp breath. She said, "That sounds—like you already know everything."
Poirot said, "Perhaps I do. He paused, then continued, "Child, can you believe that I will do everything in my power to help you?"

Indeed, they all relied on Gordon Claude. This did not mean that any family member was a parasite or idle. Jeremy Claude was a senior partner in a law firm, and Lionel Claude was a practicing physician.
However, behind the routine work and ordinary days, there was a solid financial cushion that made people feel comfortable. There was never a need for thrift or saving. The future was secure. Gordon Claude, a widower without children, would take care of everything. He had told everyone, and not just once, that it was a done deal.
His widowed sister, Adela Marchmont, might have moved into a smaller, more manageable house, but she stayed in the White House. Lin En attended elite schools. She had the opportunity to accept any expensive training she desired, thanks to the regular checks from her Gordon uncle.
Everything was so stable and safe, until Gordon Claude's unexpected marriage.
"Of course, dear," Adele continued, "we were all surprised. If there was one thing that seemed certain, it was that Gordon would never marry again, you know. He seemed to have many family ties and familial relationships."
Yes, Lynn thought, there were already enough relatives. Perhaps sometimes it would feel a little too much?
"He was always so kind and friendly," Mrs. Marchmont continued, "although he could be a little domineering at times. He never liked to eat at a table that was polished to a shine, always insisting that I put down an old-fashioned tablecloth. In fact, he even sent me a most beautiful Venetian lace tablecloth from Italy."
"It's certainly to his advantage to indulge his whims," Lynn said dryly. She then asked curiously, "How did he meet his...second wife? You didn't tell me in your letter."

Lynn was silent. It was unreasonable for her not to be upset about the latest developments, but it didn't seem to fit with Gordon's own plans. Most of his property would go to his young wife, but he would surely have made provision for the rest of the family he had always urged to rely on him. He had repeatedly advised them not to save money or make plans for the future. He had told Jeremy, "You'll be a rich man when I'm gone." He often told her mother, "Don't worry, Adela. I'll take care of Lynn - you know that, and I don't want you to move out of this house - it's your home. Send me all the repair bills."
Lynn's thoughts were interrupted by Mrs. MacIntyre dramatically producing a stack of bills, her lips trembling.
"Look at all these," she sighed. "What am I going to do? What am I going to do, Lynn? The bank manager wrote to me this morning saying I was overdrawn. I don't know how I got overdrawn. I've been so careful. But it seems my investments haven't been as profitable as they used to be. He said the taxes have gone up. And all these yellow slips - war damage insurance - you have to pay them whether you like it or not."
Lynn glanced at the bills. There were no extravagant expenses listed. They showed only the replacement of slate tiles on the roof, repairs to the fence, the replacement of the old water heater in the kitchen - and a new main water pipe. But they added up to a considerable sum.
